questions.stem: Marguerite, retired, earns $350 of net profit from occasional tutoring in 2026, her only business activity. Which statement is correct?
options: The $350 is excluded from both self-employment income and gross income
The $350 is subject to self-employment tax but no § 6017 return is required
The $350 is excluded from self-employment income but remains gross income for income tax purposes
The $350 is self-employment income because the exclusion applies only to hobby receipts
questions.explanation: IRC § 1402(b)(2) excludes net earnings below the statutory floor from self-employment income, and no § 6017 return is required; but the exclusion is from the self-employment charge, not from income tax reporting of the profit.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor asks whether her business expenses are tested under a standard different from the one that applies to a corporation's expenses. Which is correct?
options: A sole proprietor may deduct only expenses that are necessary, not merely ordinary
The ordinary and necessary standard of IRC § 162(a) applies exactly as it does to any other trade or business
Expenses are deductible only once the business has its own employer identification number
A sole proprietor deducts nothing until net earnings exceed the self-employment floor
questions.explanation: IRC § 162(a) applies as it does to any trade or business — ordinary and necessary, paid or incurred in carrying it on; there is no separate deduction standard for a sole proprietorship.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor who files a calendar-year individual return wants her bakery to report on a fiscal year ending 30 June. What taxable year does the business have?
options: Any fiscal year the owner selects on the first business schedule
A June year, because a business may adopt a natural business year
The owner's calendar year, because the business has no taxable year of its own
The calendar year for income tax but a fiscal year for self-employment tax
questions.explanation: Under Reg. § 301.7701-2(c)(2)(i) the business is disregarded and is its owner for federal tax purposes; it has no separate taxable year and adopts the owner's, just as it has no separate return or filing date.

questions.stem: A five-partner partnership that owed no tax files its Form 1065 fifteen months late, with no reasonable cause. How is the IRC § 6698 penalty computed?
options: A single flat amount for the late return
The monthly amount multiplied by five partners and by twelve months, the cap being twelve months
The monthly amount multiplied by five partners and by fifteen months
Nothing, because no tax was due
questions.explanation: IRC § 6698(b), as indexed, sets a monthly amount per person who was a partner during any part of the year, for each month the failure continues up to a maximum of twelve; the cap is on months of penalty, not on the delay, and the absence of tax is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Two unrelated individuals co-own a parcel of land held purely for appreciation, carry on no business with it, and want to keep it out of subchapter K. Which election fits?
options: The IRC § 761(f) qualified joint venture election
The IRC § 761(a) election to exclude the arrangement from subchapter K, available for an organisation availed of for investment purposes only
None; every co-ownership is a partnership and must file Form 1065
An S corporation election on Form 2553
questions.explanation: IRC § 761(a) lets all the members of an unincorporated organisation elect out of some or all of subchapter K where it is availed of for investment purposes only and not the active conduct of a business; the IRC § 761(f) election is confined to a married couple's business and would not fit.

questions.stem: Spouses jointly own a food truck. The husband runs it full time; the wife helps at a few weekend events each year. They file a joint return and both sign an election for qualified joint venture treatment. Is the election available?
options: Yes; co-ownership by spouses is enough
No; both spouses must materially participate within IRC § 469(h), and occasional weekend help is unlikely to meet any of the tests
Yes, because they file a joint return and both signed
No; a qualified joint venture may have only one spouse as owner
questions.explanation: IRC § 761(f) requires that both spouses materially participate within IRC § 469(h), determined without regard to § 469(h)(5); a joint return and a signed election satisfy the other conditions, but occasional involvement by one spouse does not satisfy this one, so the business remains a partnership.

questions.stem: A C corporation has ordinary income of $500,000 and a net capital loss of $40,000 for 2026. How is the capital loss used?
options: $3,000 is deducted against ordinary income and the balance carried forward
The whole $40,000 is deducted against ordinary income
None of it offsets ordinary income; it is carried back three years and forward five as a short-term capital loss
It is carried forward indefinitely until capital gains arise
questions.explanation: IRC § 1211(a) allows a corporation's capital losses only against capital gains, with no equivalent of the individual allowance against ordinary income, and IRC § 1212(a)(1) carries the net capital loss back three years and forward five as a short-term capital loss, earliest year first.

questions.stem: A corporation that is not a large corporation showed tax of $80,000 on its 2025 return, which covered a full twelve months. It expects 2026 tax of $120,000. What is the minimum required amount of each 2026 estimated tax installment?
questions.explanation: IRC § 6655(d)(1) sets each installment at 25 percent of the required annual payment, which is the lesser of 100 percent of the current year's tax or 100 percent of the prior year's tax; 25 percent of $80,000 is $20,000.

questions.stem: A domestic corporation that is an applicable taxpayer computes its base erosion tax for a taxable year beginning in 2026. What rate applies to modified taxable income?
options: 10 percent, the original statutory rate
10.5 percent
12.5 percent, the scheduled post-2025 rate
21 percent, the same as the regular corporate rate
questions.explanation: Pub. L. 119-21 § 70331(a)(1) substituted 10.5 percent for 10 percent in IRC § 59A(b)(1), and § 70331(a)(2) struck the paragraph that would have raised the rate for taxable years beginning after 2025, so the scheduled step-up will not happen.

questions.stem: A corporation issues voting common stock to its founders and non-voting common stock to its employees. Both classes carry identical rights to distributions and to liquidation proceeds. Does the corporation have more than one class of stock for S corporation purposes?
options: Yes; two classes of stock have been issued
No; differences in voting rights alone are disregarded
Yes, unless every shareholder consents to the S election
No, provided the corporation has 100 or fewer shareholders
questions.explanation: IRC § 1361(c)(4) disregards differences in voting power; the one-class-of-stock condition turns on rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds, which here are identical.

questions.stem: A shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation is $10,000. She has lent the corporation $15,000 and has personally guaranteed a $50,000 bank loan to it. Her share of the corporation's loss for the year is $40,000. How much may she deduct?
options: $25,000, with the $15,000 excess treated as incurred by the corporation in the following year
$25,000, with the $15,000 excess lost permanently
questions.explanation: IRC § 1366(d)(1) limits the loss to the adjusted basis of the stock plus the shareholder's basis in indebtedness of the corporation to her, $25,000 in total; a guarantee of bank debt gives no basis under IRC § 1366(d)(1)(B), and the disallowed $15,000 is treated under IRC § 1366(d)(2)(A) as incurred by the corporation in the succeeding year with respect to her.

questions.stem: A calendar-year S corporation has three shareholders holding 60, 25 and 15 percent of its shares. On 10 March 2026 the corporation files a revocation of the election with the consent of the 60 percent shareholder only, specifying no effective date. When does the election end?
options: 1 January 2026
1 January 2027
10 March 2026
It does not end, because a revocation requires the consent of every shareholder
questions.explanation: IRC § 1362(d) permits revocation consented to by shareholders holding more than one-half of the shares, and a revocation made on or before the fifteenth day of the third month of the year is retroactive to the first day of that year; 60 percent is sufficient and 10 March is within the window.

questions.stem: An LLC files Form 8832 on 1 March 2026 electing association status and specifies an effective date of 1 June 2027. From what date is the election effective?
options: 1 June 2027, as specified
1 March 2027, twelve months after filing
1 March 2026, the filing date
It is not effective at all, because the date specified is outside the window
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iii) provides that an election specifying an effective date more than 12 months after the filing date is effective 12 months after it was filed; the limit is self-correcting rather than fatal, so the election stands but takes effect on 1 March 2027.

questions.stem: An LLC formed on 1 May 2026 elects association status effective 1 May 2026, the date of its formation. In 2028 its members want to elect partnership classification. Does the 60-month bar prevent them?
options: Yes; no further election may be effective before 1 May 2031
Yes, unless more than half the ownership has changed hands
No; an election by a newly formed entity effective on the date of formation is not a change, so the 60-month clock never started
No; the bar applies only to entities that elected to be disregarded
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iv) bars a further election during the 60 months after a change of classification, and an election by a newly formed entity effective on the date of formation is not a change; the 2028 election is the entity's first change, and the clock starts then.

questions.stem: A two-member LLC has been a partnership by default since 2022. On 1 September 2026 one member buys out the other and continues alone. No form is filed. What is the LLC's classification after 1 September?
options: It remains a partnership until a Form 8832 is filed
It becomes a disregarded entity on 1 September under the default rules, with no election made and no 60-month clock started
It becomes an association, because a sole owner cannot be a partner
It remains a partnership, but must file Form 8832 within 75 days to become disregarded
questions.explanation: Under Reg. § 301.7701-3(b)(1) a domestic eligible entity with a single owner is disregarded unless it elects otherwise, so losing a member changes the classification by itself; no election is filed, none is needed, and the return that is due changes from Form 1065 to the owner's own return.

questions.stem: A calendar-year literacy charity whose gross receipts are normally about $30,000 furnishes the annual electronic notice rather than a return. By what date is the notice for 2026 due, and what penalty applies if it is late?
options: 15 April 2027, with a daily penalty for lateness
15 May 2027, with no penalty for lateness
15 May 2027, with a penalty equal to the specific deduction
31 December 2026, with no penalty for lateness
questions.explanation: IRS, Form 990-N: the notice is due by the fifteenth day of the fifth month after the year end — 15 May for a calendar-year organisation — and there is no penalty for a late submission, though under IRC § 6033(j) three consecutive missed notices still cost the exemption.

questions.stem: The board of a § 501(c)(3) organisation asks which of the restrictions on its conduct is a matter of degree rather than an absolute bar. Which is correct?
options: Inurement of net earnings is tolerated below a substantiality threshold
Campaign intervention is permitted if it is insubstantial
Only the lobbying restriction turns on whether the activity is a substantial part of its activities
All four conditions apply only to substantial violations
questions.explanation: IRC § 501(c)(3): no substantial part of the activities may be lobbying, so only that condition is a matter of degree; inurement and campaign intervention have no threshold at all.

questions.stem: A community food bank organised in 2024 first gives notice under IRC § 508(a) in 2026 that it is applying for recognition as a § 501(c)(3) organisation. For what period is it treated as described in § 501(c)(3)?
options: From its 2024 organisation date, because the notice relates back
Only from the time the notice is given
From the start of the tax year in which the notice was given
It is never treated as described in § 501(c)(3) because the notice was late
questions.explanation: IRC § 508(a) makes the notice a condition of being treated as described in § 501(c)(3) at all, and a late notice operates prospectively — not for any period before it is given — which is why the effective date on the recognition letter matters to donors.

questions.stem: A foreign eligible entity has a single owner who has limited liability under the law of the country where the entity is organised. No Form 8832 is filed. How is the entity classified?
options: Disregarded, like a domestic single-owner entity
A partnership
An association, because its only member has limited liability
Unclassified until an election is filed
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.7701-3(b)(2)(i)(B) classifies a foreign eligible entity as an association if all its members have limited liability; a single-owner foreign entity is disregarded only where that owner lacks limited liability, which is the reverse of the domestic default.
questions.pageTitle: Entity type default classifications and elections

questions.stem: A partnership holds property with an aggregate adjusted basis of $500,000, subject to $620,000 of liabilities. It elects association status effective 1 January 2027. What gain does the deemed contribution produce?
options: None; the deemed contribution is a tax-free exchange under IRC § 351
$120,000 of gain, the excess of liabilities assumed over the basis of the property transferred
Gain equal to the property's fair market value less its basis, as on a liquidation
$620,000 of gain, the full amount of the liabilities assumed
questions.explanation: Under Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(1)(i) the partnership is deemed to contribute its assets and liabilities to the association for stock; the exchange falls within IRC § 351, but IRC § 357(c)(1) treats the $120,000 by which liabilities assumed exceed the aggregate basis of the property as gain from the sale or exchange of property.
questions.pageTitle: Entity type default classifications and elections

questions.stem: A corporation owns all the stock of a subsidiary that is an association, and elects on Form 8832 to have the subsidiary disregarded. What is the tax result of the deemed liquidation?
options: The association recognises gain under IRC § 336 and the parent under IRC § 331, with no relief available
The parent may reach nonrecognition under IRC § 332, the regulation supplying the deemed adoption of a plan of liquidation
No deemed transaction occurs, because the subsidiary was wholly owned
The parent must first adopt a formal plan of liquidation or the election is void
questions.explanation: A corporate parent whose stock ownership meets the IRC § 1504(a)(2) test may reach nonrecognition on the receipt of the property under IRC § 332(a), (b)(1), and Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(2)(ii) treats the association as adopting a plan of liquidation immediately before the deemed liquidation so that condition of IRC § 332 is met.
questions.pageTitle: Entity type default classifications and elections

questions.stem: Ines has run a bakery as a sole proprietor for four years, reporting on Schedule C under her social security number. In 2026 she hires her first employee. What number goes on the bakery's Form 941?
options: Her social security number, because a sole proprietor is an individual
An employer identification number; an individual who is an employer is directed to use one
Either number, at her choice
An individual taxpayer identification number obtained for the business
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(ii)(D) directs a sole proprietor who is an employer, or who is engaged in a trade or business, to use an employer identification number where the form calls for one; the option that a sole proprietor is limited to a social security number is the trap.

questions.stem: A corporation lets its charter lapse, and its shareholders then obtain a new charter from the secretary of state for a corporation carrying on the same business with the same assets and the same shareholders. Does it need a new employer identification number?
options: No, because the business and the owners are the same
No, provided the name and the address are also unchanged
Yes; a corporation that receives a new charter from the secretary of state needs a new number
Yes, but only if it also elects S corporation status
questions.explanation: On the IRS guidance, Do you need a new EIN?, a corporation needs a new number on receiving a new charter from the secretary of state, because the State has created a different legal person, even though the business is identical.

questions.stem: A subsidiary corporation applies for an employer identification number. Which of the following may be named as its responsible party on Form SS-4?
options: The parent corporation, as owner of all the shares
The registered-agent service that filed the formation documents
The subsidiary's principal officer, who controls its funds and assets
The law firm holding the shares until closing
questions.explanation: On the IRS guidance on responsible parties and nominees, the responsible party must own, control or exercise effective control over the entity and must be an individual rather than an entity, except for government entities; a parent company cannot be named, and a formation agent or a lawyer holding shares temporarily is a nominee.

questions.stem: A partnership has three partners. Alder holds 60 percent of profits but 30 percent of capital and uses a year ending 30 June. Birch and Cedar each hold 20 percent of profits and 35 percent of capital and use the calendar year. What is the partnership's required year?
options: 30 June, because Alder holds a majority of profits
30 June, because Alder is the largest single partner
The calendar year, because no majority interest year exists and the principal partners do not all share a year
Whichever year the partnership prefers, since the tests conflict
questions.explanation: The majority interest test under IRC § 706(b)(4)(A)(i) requires more than half of profits and capital in aggregate, and no group of partners with a common year holds both; all three are principal partners under IRC § 706(b)(3) but do not share a year, so the calendar year applies.

questions.stem: A newly formed partnership whose required year is the calendar year makes a section 444 election at formation for a year ending 31 October. What is the deferral period of the elected year?
options: One month
Two months
Three months
Ten months
questions.explanation: IRC § 444(b)(4) measures the deferral period from the beginning of the elected year, 1 November, to the close of the first required year ending within it, 31 December, which is two months; that is within the three-month cap of IRC § 444(b)(1).

questions.stem: A partnership whose partners are all calendar-year individuals asks for a year ending 31 January, on the stated ground that the partners would like to defer eleven months of income. On what basis is the request decided?
options: Granted, because a business purpose is any reason the partners give
Granted, provided every partner consents in writing
Refused; deferral of income to partners is expressly not a business purpose
Granted under a section 444 election, since the deferral period is one month
questions.explanation: IRC § 706(b)(1)(C) says in terms that deferral of income to partners is never a business purpose; a 31 January year would also carry an eleven-month deferral period, far beyond the three-month cap that section 444 imposes.

questions.stem: A corporation has kept its books on the accrual basis for years and filed on that basis. For 2026 its controller wants to file on the cash method to defer income, without filing any request. Is that permitted?
options: Yes, because a taxpayer may choose its method on each year's return
Yes, provided the corporation meets the gross receipts test
No; the method for tax is the method on which the books are kept, and switching without consent is an unconsented change
Yes, provided a second set of cash-basis books is kept alongside the first
questions.explanation: IRC § 446(a) attaches the tax method to the method regularly used in keeping the books, and IRC § 446(e) requires consent before a change; there is no annual election, so filing on a different basis is an unconsented change of method.

questions.stem: Two corporations under common control each have average annual gross receipts of $20 million for 2023 to 2025, or $40 million between them. Each is otherwise an ordinary C corporation. For 2026, may either use the cash method?
options: Yes; each is under the threshold on its own figures
No; commonly controlled entities are aggregated for the test, and the combined receipts exceed the 2026 figure
Yes, provided each keeps separate and complete books
No, because a C corporation may never use the cash method
questions.explanation: IRC § 448(c)(2) aggregates gross receipts across commonly controlled entities, so splitting a business into two entities does not split the receipts; at $40 million combined the test is failed and IRC § 448(a)(1) prohibits the cash method for both.

questions.stem: An accrual-basis employer's liability under a workers compensation claim becomes fixed and determinable in December 2026 at $75,000, payable in monthly instalments beginning February 2027. How much may it deduct for 2026?
options: The full $75,000, because the all events test is satisfied
The full $75,000 under the recurring item exception, since payments begin within 8½ months of year end
Nothing beyond amounts actually paid in 2026, because economic performance for a workers compensation liability occurs as payments are made
The full $75,000, provided the amount is immaterial
questions.explanation: Under IRC § 461(h) economic performance for a workers compensation liability occurs as the payments are made, and IRC § 461(h)(3) expressly leaves workers compensation and tort liabilities outside the recurring item exception, so the all events test alone does not support a 2026 deduction.

questions.stem: A dental practice pays $2,600 of rent during calendar year 2026 to an individual who owns its premises. Must the practice file an information return for the payment?
options: No; rent is not a payment within IRC § 6041(a)
Yes; rent paid in the course of a trade or business is within IRC § 6041(a), and $2,600 reaches the 2026 amount
No; only nonemployee compensation is reportable
Yes, but only if the landlord is a corporation
questions.explanation: IRC § 6041(a) requires a return from a person engaged in a trade or business who pays rent or other fixed or determinable income of the applicable amount or more in a calendar year, and $2,600 is above the raised 2026 figure; payments to a corporation are the ones generally outside the section, not payments to an individual.
questions.pageTitle: Reporting requirements (e.g. Forms W2, W-4, Form 1099)

questions.stem: A business files Forms W-2 and Forms 1099-NEC for calendar year 2026. By what date must they be filed?
options: 31 January 2027
28 February 2027
31 March 2027
15 April 2027
questions.explanation: IRC § 6071(b), (c) requires Forms W-2 and W-3 and any return reporting nonemployee compensation to be filed on or before 31 January of the year following the calendar year; the 31 March date applies to other information returns filed electronically, not to these.
questions.pageTitle: Reporting requirements (e.g. Forms W2, W-4, Form 1099)

questions.stem: A third party settlement organisation processes $18,000 for a participating payee across 350 transactions in 2026. Which statement is correct?
options: A Form 1099-K is required, because the transaction count is exceeded
No Form 1099-K is required, because the dollar limb is not exceeded, and the payee's income is taxable regardless
No Form 1099-K is required, so the payee need not report the income
A Form 1099-K is required, because exceeding either limb is enough
questions.explanation: IRC § 6050W(e) as restored requires both the amount and the transaction count to be exceeded, so the dollar limb alone defeats reporting here; the threshold governs the payer's obligation and not the payee's return, so the income is fully taxable whether or not a form arrives.
questions.pageTitle: Reporting requirements (e.g. Forms W2, W-4, Form 1099)

questions.stem: Under IRC § 183(c), an activity is "not engaged in for profit" when:
options: It has produced losses in three or more of the last five years
Deductions are not allowable for it under IRC § 162 or under IRC § 212
The taxpayer has substantial income from other sources
It has elements of personal pleasure or recreation
questions.explanation: IRC § 183(c) defines the term by exclusion: an activity is not engaged in for profit if deductions are not allowable for it under IRC § 162 or § 212, so the question is whether it is a trade or business or an income-producing activity under those sections, and IRC § 183 is a consequence rather than a test.
questions.pageTitle: Hobby versus business determination and loss limitations

questions.stem: A horse breeding activity produced net income in 2021 and 2025 and losses in 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2026. Does the IRC § 183(d) presumption apply for 2026?
options: No; fewer than three of the last five years were profitable
Yes; for a horse activity the test is two profitable years out of the seven ending with 2026, and 2021 and 2025 meet it
No; the two profitable years must be consecutive
Yes; any activity with two profitable years qualifies
questions.explanation: IRC § 183(d) substitutes two of seven consecutive years for three of five where the activity consists in major part of breeding, training, showing or racing horses; the seven years ending with 2026 run from 2020, and 2021 and 2025 are two profitable years within them.
questions.pageTitle: Hobby versus business determination and loss limitations

questions.stem: A couple plant an orchard on land they bought for the purpose, expecting operating losses for at least ten years but substantial appreciation in the land. Does the expected appreciation count toward a profit objective?
options: No; only expected operating income counts
No; land appreciation is investment return, not income from the activity
Yes; profit for this purpose includes appreciation in the value of assets used in the activity, including land
Only if the land is sold within the five-year presumption window
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.183-2(b)(4) treats profit as encompassing appreciation in the value of assets used in the activity, including land, so the couple may intend an overall profit even though current operations will lose money for years.
questions.pageTitle: Hobby versus business determination and loss limitations

questions.stem: A partnership holds one parcel of land as an investment for six years and sells it at a $400,000 gain. One partner is a full-time real estate dealer; the other is a retired nurse. How is each partner's share characterised?
options: Capital gain for both
Ordinary income for the dealer and capital gain for the nurse
Ordinary income for both
Whatever character each partner's own activities would give it
questions.explanation: IRC § 702(b) determines character as if the partner had realised the item directly from the source from which the partnership realised it, and the partnership held the parcel as an investment; the dealer's personal status is not the source.
questions.pageTitle: Partnership income, expenses, distributions, and flow-through (e.g.,self- employment income)

questions.stem: A partner's distributive share of loss has cleared the IRC § 704(d) basis limitation. Which limitation is applied next?
options: The at-risk rules
The passive activity rules
The excess business loss limitation
None, because basis is the only gate
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(d) is the first of several gates; the loss must then survive the at-risk rules, then the passive activity rules, then the excess business loss limitation, in that order.
questions.pageTitle: Partnership income, expenses, distributions, and flow-through (e.g.,self- employment income)

questions.stem: Clementine contributes $10,000 of cash for her interest. The partnership then borrows $200,000, of which her share is $50,000. Her outside basis is:
questions.explanation: IRC § 752 treats a partner's share of partnership liabilities as money contributed, so her basis includes the $50,000 of borrowing she never made personally on top of the $10,000 of cash.
questions.pageTitle: Partnership income, expenses, distributions, and flow-through (e.g.,self- employment income)

questions.stem: A parent gives a child a 20 percent capital interest in a manufacturing partnership, keeping 80 percent, and is paid reasonable compensation for managing it. The agreement then allocates 40 percent of the remaining profits to the child. Is the child's share respected?
options: Yes, because reasonable compensation to the parent has already been allowed
No, because the child's share for donated capital is proportionately greater than the parent's share for the parent's own capital
Yes, because partners are free to agree any profit split
No, because a gift-derived partner may not share in profits at all
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(e)(1) imposes two limits that operate together: after reasonable compensation to the donor, the donee's share attributable to donated capital may not be proportionately greater than the donor's share attributable to the donor's capital.

questions.stem: A taxpayer sells a capital interest in the family business to her brother for full fair market value. Is the interest treated as created by gift?
options: Yes, because any sale between relatives is treated as a gift
No, because siblings are outside the definition of family for this purpose
Yes, unless the price is full fair market value
No, because the sale was for cash rather than a promissory note
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(e)(2) treats an intra-family purchase as a gift, but family there reaches only the spouse, ancestors, lineal descendants and trusts primarily for their benefit; a brother is outside it.

questions.stem: A parent gives her daughter a right to 20 percent of the profits of an inventory-heavy wholesale business, with no right to any assets on withdrawal or liquidation. Does the daughter hold a capital interest?
options: Yes, because capital is a material income-producing factor in the business
No: a capital interest is an interest in assets distributable on withdrawal or liquidation, and a mere right to share in profits is not one
Yes, because a daughter is a lineal descendant
No, because profits interests may only be given to a spouse
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.704-1(e)(1)(v) defines a capital interest as an interest in the assets of the partnership distributable to its owner on withdrawal or liquidation, and the mere right to participate in earnings and profits is not one.

questions.stem: A partnership agrees to pay Rosalind, for her services, the greater of $80,000 or 20 percent of net profits. Net profits before the payment are $600,000 and she receives $120,000. How much is a guaranteed payment?
options: Nothing, because the amount depended on profits
questions.explanation: IRC § 707(c): only the $80,000 minimum is determined without regard to the income of the partnership; the $40,000 excess varies with profits and is a distributive share allocated under IRC § 704.
questions.pageTitle: Partner's dealings with partnership (e.g., exchange of property, guaranteed payments)

questions.stem: Tobias owns a 65 percent capital interest in a partnership that holds land as inventory for resale. He sells it a parcel he has held for investment for ten years, realising a $50,000 gain. The gain is:
options: Ordinary income, because the parcel is not a capital asset in the partnership's hands
Long-term capital gain, because it was a capital asset in his hands
Not recognised until the partnership resells the parcel
Long-term capital gain, because he owns less than 80 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 707(b)(2): a gain on a sale between a partnership and a person owning more than 50 percent of its capital or profits interest is ordinary income where the property is other than a capital asset in the hands of the transferee, and the character in the seller's hands is irrelevant.
questions.pageTitle: Partner's dealings with partnership (e.g., exchange of property, guaranteed payments)

questions.stem: Ines owns exactly 50 percent of the capital and profits of a partnership. She sells it equipment at a $30,000 loss. Is the loss allowed?
options: Yes, because IRC § 707(b)(1) applies only to a partner owning more than 50 percent
No, it is disallowed under IRC § 707(b)(1)
No, it is deferred until the partnership disposes of the equipment
Yes, but only half of it, matching her interest
questions.explanation: IRC § 707(b)(1) disallows a loss only where the partner owns, directly or indirectly, more than 50 percent of the capital or profits interest; a partner with exactly half is outside the provision.
questions.pageTitle: Partner's dealings with partnership (e.g., exchange of property, guaranteed payments)

questions.stem: Twenty years after a partnership was formed, an outsider contributes appreciated land in exchange for a 2 percent interest. No other partner contributes anything at the same time. Is the contribution taxable?
options: Yes, because the contributor does not control the partnership afterwards
Yes, because the other partners did not contribute at the same time
No: nonrecognition applies without any control, timing or percentage test
Yes, to the extent of the built-in gain, unless every partner consents
questions.explanation: IRC § 721(a) has no analogue of the corporate control requirement, so a contribution qualifies whether the contributor ends up with one percent or ninety-nine and whether they join at formation or twenty years later.
questions.pageTitle: Contribution of property and/or services to partnership (e.g., partnership's basis, property subject to indebtedness)

questions.stem: A partner contributes property worth $500,000 with an adjusted basis of $200,000 for a 50 percent interest. The partnership later sells it for $560,000. How much of the gain is allocated to the contributing partner?
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(c)(1)(A) allocates the $300,000 pre-contribution variation between basis and value to the contributor alone; only the $60,000 of post-contribution appreciation is shared, and half of that is $30,000.
questions.pageTitle: Contribution of property and/or services to partnership (e.g., partnership's basis, property subject to indebtedness)

questions.stem: A partner contributes a capital asset with a basis of $300,000 and a value of $200,000. The partnership holds it as inventory and sells it three years later for $150,000. What is the character of the $150,000 loss?
options: All $150,000 capital
$100,000 capital and $50,000 ordinary
All $150,000 ordinary
$100,000 ordinary and $50,000 capital
questions.explanation: IRC § 724(c) keeps a built-in capital loss capital for five years, but only to the extent of the loss that existed at contribution; the further $50,000 decline after contribution takes the property's character in the partnership's hands.
questions.pageTitle: Contribution of property and/or services to partnership (e.g., partnership's basis, property subject to indebtedness)

questions.stem: A partner begins the year with an outside basis of $40,000. During the year the partnership distributes $30,000 of cash to him and allocates him a $25,000 loss. What is the result?
options: He deducts $25,000 and recognises $15,000 of gain on the distribution
He takes the $30,000 tax-free, deducts $10,000, and carries $15,000 of loss forward
He deducts $25,000 and takes the distribution tax-free, leaving a negative basis
He deducts nothing, because the distribution exceeded the loss
questions.explanation: Distributions reduce basis under IRC § 733 before losses are tested under IRC § 704(d), so basis falls to $10,000 tax-free and the loss is allowed only to that extent, with the balance suspended under IRC § 704(d)(2).

questions.stem: A new partner contributes $100,000 of cash for a 25 percent interest in a partnership that carries $400,000 of recourse debt shared in proportion to interests. What is her outside basis immediately after admission?
options: $100,000, rising only when she becomes personally liable on the debt
questions.explanation: IRC § 752(a) treats her $100,000 share of partnership liabilities as a contribution of money, so it adds to the $100,000 of cash she contributed under IRC § 722 whether or not she is personally liable.

questions.stem: A partner has $20,000 of losses suspended under IRC § 704(d). In the following year he is allocated no income, but the partnership borrows and his share of its liabilities rises by $35,000. What happens to the suspended loss?
options: It stays suspended, because only allocated income restores basis
It is allowed in full, because the liability increase is a deemed contribution that restores basis
It is allowed only to the extent of $15,000
It is lost permanently at the end of the year in which it was suspended
questions.explanation: The increase in his share of liabilities is a deemed contribution of money under IRC § 752(a), and IRC § 704(d)(2) allows a suspended loss when basis is restored — by a liability increase as readily as by income.

questions.stem: A partnership holds no receivables and no inventory, but owns fully depreciated equipment worth well above its written-down cost. A partner sells his interest at a gain. What is the character of the gain?
options: All capital, because the partnership has no receivables or inventory
Part ordinary, because unrealized receivables include the recapture on the equipment
All ordinary, because the partnership holds depreciable property
All capital, unless an IRC § 754 election is in effect
questions.explanation: IRC § 751(c) extends unrealized receivables to IRC § 1245 property to the extent of the recapture, so a partnership with depreciated equipment has hot assets and IRC § 751(a) treats that part of the amount received as ordinary.

questions.stem: A partner's outside basis is $120,000, including a $50,000 share of partnership liabilities. She sells her interest for $140,000 of cash and the buyer takes over her share of the debt. Her share of the ordinary income embedded in the partnership's unrealized receivables is $60,000. What does she report?
options: $20,000 of capital gain
$70,000 of capital gain
$60,000 of ordinary income and $10,000 of capital gain
$60,000 of ordinary income and a $40,000 capital loss
questions.explanation: The amount realised is $190,000 once the $50,000 of relieved liabilities is added under IRC § 752(b); IRC § 751(a) takes $60,000 as ordinary, and the residual $130,000 against her $120,000 basis is a $10,000 capital gain under IRC § 741.

questions.stem: A buyer pays far more for a partnership interest than her share of the partnership's inside basis and wants that basis adjusted. Who can make the IRC § 754 election, and for how long does it apply?
options: The buyer, by filing it with her own return for the year of purchase
The partnership, and it then applies to all transfers and distributions in that year and every subsequent year
The partnership, for this transfer only, and it lapses the following year
Nobody; the adjustment is automatic whenever the price exceeds inside basis
questions.explanation: The IRC § 754 election is made by the partnership, not the buyer, and it is not revocable at will: it applies to all distributions and transfers in the year filed and in every subsequent year, which is why partnerships hesitate to make it.

questions.stem: A partnership incurs $53,000 of organizational expenses and begins business in March 2026. It makes the IRC § 709(b) election. What does it deduct?
options: $2,000 immediately and $51,000 rateably over 180 months from March 2026
$5,000 immediately and $48,000 rateably over 180 months
Nothing immediately and $53,000 rateably over 180 months
$5,000 immediately and $48,000 rateably over 60 months
questions.explanation: IRC § 709(b)(1): the immediate deduction is reduced dollar for dollar by the amount by which the expenses exceed the higher threshold, which they do by $3,000, and the remainder is amortised over 180 months beginning with the month business begins.
questions.pageTitle: Partnership formation (e.g., partnership agreement, general vs. limited partners, capital contributions)

questions.stem: A partnership is organised and files its certificate in October 2026 but does not begin business until February 2027. It elects under IRC § 709(b). Its 180-month amortisation period begins in:
options: February 2027
October 2026
January 2027, the start of its first full year
The month its first return is filed
questions.explanation: IRC § 709(b)(1) runs the 180-month period from the month in which the partnership begins business, not from the month it is organised.
questions.pageTitle: Partnership formation (e.g., partnership agreement, general vs. limited partners, capital contributions)

questions.stem: Which of these costs is an organizational expense eligible for the IRC § 709(b) election?
options: An accountant's fee for setting up the partnership's books
A placement agent's commission on the sale of limited partnership interests
Registration fees for the offering of interests
Printing costs of the offering memorandum
questions.explanation: IRC § 709(b)(3) defines an organizational expense as one incident to the creation of the partnership; the other three are incurred to promote the sale of interests and are syndication costs that IRC § 709(a) denies any deduction for.
questions.pageTitle: Partnership formation (e.g., partnership agreement, general vs. limited partners, capital contributions)

questions.stem: One of the two partners in a partnership buys the other's entire interest and carries on the same business alone as a sole proprietor. Does the partnership terminate?
options: No, because the business continues without interruption
Yes, because no part of the business continues to be carried on by any partner in a partnership
No, because only 50 percent of the interests changed hands
Yes, because 50 percent or more of the interests were sold within twelve months
questions.explanation: IRC § 708(b)(1) terminates a partnership only where no part of its business continues to be carried on by any of its partners in a partnership, and a single owner cannot carry on in a partnership.
questions.pageTitle: Dissolution of partnership (e.g., sale, death of partner)

questions.stem: A partner sells half of her interest to a new partner on 1 July 2026, keeping the other half. Does the partnership's taxable year close with respect to her?
options: Yes, for the half she sold
No; the year closes with respect to a partner only when their entire interest terminates
Yes, and for the whole partnership as well
Yes, with respect to both her and the buyer
questions.explanation: IRC § 706(c)(2)(B) is explicit that the year does not close with respect to a partner who disposes of less than their entire interest; only an entire termination under IRC § 706(c)(2)(A) closes it.
questions.pageTitle: Dissolution of partnership (e.g., sale, death of partner)

questions.stem: A retiring limited partner in a partnership in which capital is not a material income-producing factor is paid $300,000 for her share of unrealized receivables. How is the payment treated?
options: As an IRC § 736(a) payment, because capital is not a material income-producing factor
As an IRC § 736(b) payment, because the carve-out also requires that the retiring partner was a general partner
As an IRC § 736(a) payment, because payments for receivables are always ordinary income
Half under each subsection
questions.explanation: IRC § 736(b)(3) applies the receivables and goodwill carve-outs only where both conditions are met — capital not material and the partner a general partner — so for a limited partner the payment stays within IRC § 736(b).
questions.pageTitle: Dissolution of partnership (e.g., sale, death of partner)

questions.stem: A partnership uses a fiscal year ending 30 June 2026 and obtains no extension. Its Form 1065 for that year is due on:
options: 15 September 2026
15 October 2026
15 March 2027
15 April 2027
questions.explanation: IRC § 6072(b): the return is due the fifteenth day of the third month following the close of the fiscal year, and the third month after June is September.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, due dates, penalties, and audit notice requirements

questions.stem: A calendar-year partnership with four partners extends its 2026 Form 1065 to 15 September 2027 and files on 20 September 2027. For how many partner-months is the penalty charged?
options: Four
Twenty-four
Twenty-eight
None, because the return was filed within the extension period
questions.explanation: IRC § 6698(a)(1) measures the failure from the due date determined with regard to any extension, so lateness runs from 16 September; 16 to 20 September is a fraction of a month counted as a whole one, giving one month multiplied by four partners.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, due dates, penalties, and audit notice requirements

questions.stem: A partnership has never designated a partnership representative and comes under examination for its 2026 year. Which is correct?
options: The Service may select any person to serve as the partnership representative
The partner with the largest profits interest is the representative by default
The examination cannot proceed until the partnership designates one
Each partner deals with the Service on their own behalf
questions.explanation: IRC § 6223(a): each partnership must designate a representative, and where no designation is in effect the Service may select any person, who then has sole authority to act for the partnership.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, due dates, penalties, and audit notice requirements

questions.stem: A partnership is insolvent by $2,000,000 when a lender forgives $450,000 of its debt. Partner Ludovic, allocated $150,000 of the discharge income, has personal net assets of $900,000 after counting his share of partnership liabilities. Ludovic must include:
options: $150,000, because he is not himself insolvent
Nothing, because the partnership is insolvent
Nothing, because his share of the partnership's insolvency exceeds $150,000
$150,000, but deferred until the partnership becomes solvent
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(d)(6) applies the insolvency exclusion at the partner level, so the test is whether the partner is insolvent on his own liabilities and assets; a solvent partner in an insolvent partnership excludes nothing.

questions.stem: Perpetua's outside basis is $20,000. She is allocated $60,000 of partnership discharge income, none of which she can exclude, and her share of partnership liabilities falls by $60,000. What gain does she recognise under IRC § 731(a)(1)?
options: None
questions.explanation: IRC § 705(a)(1)(A) increases her basis by the $60,000 of included income to $80,000 before the IRC § 752(b) deemed distribution of $60,000 reduces it to $20,000; because the income was taxed rather than excluded, the two movements offset and no basis is exceeded.

questions.stem: In March 2026 a lender discharges qualified principal residence indebtedness. No written arrangement for the discharge existed before 2026. Is the IRC § 108(a)(1)(E) exclusion available?
options: No, it reaches only a discharge before 1 January 2026 or one under a written arrangement entered into before that date
Yes, the exclusion has no expiry
Yes, for any discharge before 1 January 2027
Yes, but only if applied at the partnership level
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(a)(1)(E) by its own terms covers only a discharge occurring before 1 January 2026, or one made under a written arrangement entered into before that date, and the primary window has closed.

questions.stem: A partnership validly elected out of the centralised regime on its timely 2025 return. Nothing about its partners has changed. For 2026 it:
options: Must make the election again on a timely filed 2026 return
Remains outside the regime automatically
Remains outside the regime for five years
Need only notify its partners that the election continues
questions.explanation: IRC § 6221(b) provides no continuing election; the election is annual and must be made again each year on a timely filed return with the required disclosures.

questions.stem: Adjustments for a reviewed year total $1,000,000, of which 40 percent was allocable to a tax-exempt partner. That partner files a return taking its share into account under the modification procedures, with no tax due. The imputed underpayment is computed on:
options: Nothing, because one partner has filed
questions.explanation: IRC § 6225(c)(2)(A): where a reviewed-year partner files a return taking its allocable adjustments into account and pays any tax due, the imputed underpayment is determined without regard to the portion so taken into account, removing the 40 percent.

questions.stem: A partnership has five partners: four individuals and a single-member LLC that is disregarded for tax purposes and owned by an individual. May the partnership elect out under IRC § 6221(b)?
options: No, because a disregarded entity is not an eligible partner
Yes, because the LLC's owner is an individual
Yes, provided fewer than 100 statements are furnished
Yes, if the LLC consents to the election
questions.explanation: IRC § 6221(b)(1)(C) lists the eligible partner types exhaustively — individuals, C corporations, foreign entities that would be C corporations, S corporations and estates of deceased partners — and a disregarded entity holding an interest disqualifies the election regardless of who owns it.

questions.stem: A calendar-year C corporation files Form 7004 on 15 April 2027 for its 2026 return and remits its properly estimated unpaid liability. To what date is the return extended, and is the payment date extended with it?
options: 15 October 2027; the payment date is extended to the same day
15 October 2027; the payment date is not extended
15 September 2027; the payment date is not extended
15 November 2027; the payment date is extended to the same day
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.6081-3(a) gives an automatic six-month extension from the IRC § 6072(a) fourth-month date, but Reg. § 1.6081-3(b) makes it an extension of time to file only, so the failure-to-pay addition runs from the unextended payment date.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, due dates, and penalties

questions.stem: A calendar-year C corporation with $20,000 of tax shown files its return and pays the tax 40 days after the unextended due date, with no extension and no reasonable cause. What is the total addition under IRC § 6651?
questions.explanation: IRC § 6651(a)(1) charges 5 percent for each month or fraction of a month — two months here — on the tax required to be shown, and IRC § 6651(c)(1) reduces it by the 0.5 percent failure-to-pay addition for each overlapping month, so the total is $2,000 rather than $2,200.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, due dates, and penalties

questions.stem: A dormant calendar-year C corporation and a dormant partnership with four partners each file ten months late; neither owes any tax. Which faces a late-filing penalty?
options: Both, at the minimum addition for a return more than 60 days late
Neither, because there is no tax
Only the partnership, because IRC § 6698 measures the penalty in partners and months rather than tax
Only the corporation, because partnerships are not penalised for late returns
questions.explanation: Both IRC § 6651(a) additions are percentages of tax, and the minimum addition is capped at 100 percent of the tax required to be shown, so the corporation owes nothing; the IRC § 6698 partnership penalty is measured in partners and months.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, due dates, and penalties

questions.stem: A corporation has current earnings and profits of $50,000 and accumulated earnings and profits of $30,000. It distributes $130,000 in cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $60,000. What is the character of the distribution?
options: $80,000 dividend and $50,000 return of capital
$50,000 dividend, $60,000 return of capital and $20,000 gain
$130,000 dividend
$80,000 dividend, $30,000 return of capital and $20,000 gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 316(a) makes the distribution a dividend to the extent of current earnings and profits first and then accumulated — $80,000 in total — and the remaining $50,000 is a return of capital against the $60,000 basis, so no gain arises.

questions.stem: A corporation distributes to its shareholders its own $200,000 promissory note and a parcel of land with an adjusted basis of $140,000 and a fair market value of $140,000. By how much are its earnings and profits reduced?
options: Nil, because no cash left the corporation
questions.explanation: IRC § 312(a) reduces earnings and profits by the principal amount of the corporation's own obligations and by the adjusted basis of other property distributed, so $200,000 plus $140,000; the IRC § 312(b) fair market value rule applies only to appreciated property.

questions.stem: A corporation distributes $90,000 on 1 March 2026. At that date it has no accumulated earnings and profits and has earned nothing so far in the year; by 31 December 2026 its current earnings and profits total $120,000. How is the March distribution treated?
options: A return of capital, because there were no earnings and profits on 1 March
A dividend in full, because current earnings and profits are computed as of the close of the year
A dividend only to the extent of earnings and profits earned by 1 March
Gain from the sale or exchange of the stock
questions.explanation: IRC § 316(a)(2) makes a distribution a dividend to the extent of the earnings and profits of the taxable year computed as of the close of the year, without regard to the amount on hand when the distribution was made.

questions.stem: A corporation offers each common shareholder the choice of receiving the year's distribution either in additional common shares or in cash. Hesper elects shares worth $10,000. What is the treatment?
options: Excluded from gross income under IRC § 305(a) as a stock dividend
Treated as an IRC § 301 distribution, because a distribution payable at the shareholder's election in stock or property is an IRC § 305(b) exception
A return of capital, because no cash left the corporation
Taxable only when the shares are sold
questions.explanation: IRC § 305(a) excludes a stock dividend, but IRC § 305(b) makes an exception where the distribution is payable at any shareholder's election in stock or in property; it is then treated as an IRC § 301 distribution and runs through the ordinary tiers.
questions.pageTitle: Shareholder dividends, distributions, and recognition requirements

questions.stem: A corporation with ample earnings and profits distributes a warehouse worth $500,000, subject to a $560,000 mortgage that the shareholder assumes. What is the amount distributed under IRC § 301(b)?
options: Negative $60,000, creating a deduction for the shareholder
$500,000, because liabilities do not affect the amount
Nil, because the liability reduces the amount but not below zero
questions.explanation: IRC § 301(b)(2) reduces the amount distributed by liabilities the shareholder assumes or that encumber the property received, but never below zero.
questions.pageTitle: Shareholder dividends, distributions, and recognition requirements

questions.stem: A corporation intends to put a machine worth $100,000 with an adjusted basis of $400,000 into its sole shareholder's hands. Which approach preserves the $300,000 loss?
options: Distribute the machine; IRC § 311(a) lets the corporation recognise the loss
Distribute the machine; the shareholder inherits the $400,000 basis and recognises the loss on a later sale
Sell the machine for $100,000, recognise the loss, and distribute the cash
Neither; a loss on corporate property is never deductible
questions.explanation: IRC § 311(a) denies the corporation any loss on distributing depreciated property and IRC § 301(d) gives the shareholder fair market value as basis, so a distribution destroys the loss; a sale followed by a cash distribution recognises it.
questions.pageTitle: Shareholder dividends, distributions, and recognition requirements

questions.stem: A corporation's taxable income before the dividends received deduction is $200,000, including $300,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it holds 10 percent. What deduction is allowed?
questions.explanation: IRC § 246(b) caps the deduction at 50 percent of taxable income computed before the deduction, $100,000, and IRC § 246(b)(2) does not lift the cap because the full $150,000 deduction would leave $50,000 of taxable income rather than a net operating loss.
questions.pageTitle: Special deductions and credits (e.g., dividends received deduction, charitable deduction)

questions.stem: A corporation owns 30 percent of another corporation's voting power but only 12 percent of its value, and receives a $50,000 dividend. What rate of dividends received deduction applies?
options: 65 percent, because voting power exceeds 20 percent
50 percent, because the 20-percent test requires both vote and value
100 percent, because the corporations are affiliated
65 percent, averaged from the two percentages
questions.explanation: IRC § 243(c)(2) defines a 20-percent owned corporation by 20 percent or more of the stock by vote and value — the test is conjunctive — so the default IRC § 243(a)(1) rate of 50 percent applies.
questions.pageTitle: Special deductions and credits (e.g., dividends received deduction, charitable deduction)

questions.stem: A corporation with taxable income of $2,000,000 makes $150,000 of charitable contributions in a taxable year beginning in 2026. What is deductible?
options: Nil, because the contributions are under 10 percent of taxable income
questions.explanation: IRC § 170(b)(2)(A), as rewritten by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70426 for taxable years beginning after 2025, allows the deduction only to the extent contributions exceed 1 percent of taxable income — $20,000 — and only up to 10 percent, so $130,000 is deductible.
questions.pageTitle: Special deductions and credits (e.g., dividends received deduction, charitable deduction)

questions.stem: Ludovic owns 300 of a corporation's 1,000 voting shares; his sister owns 400 and his father owns 300. The corporation redeems all of Ludovic's shares. After the redemption, how many shares is he treated as owning for the purpose of IRC § 302(b)(3)?
options: 700, the shares of both relatives
300, his father's shares only
400, his sister's shares only
Nil, because he holds none directly
questions.explanation: IRC § 318(a)(1) attributes stock owned by a spouse, children, grandchildren and parents, but there is no attribution between siblings, so he is treated as owning his father's 300 shares and his interest has not been completely terminated.

questions.stem: Ottoline owns 8,000 of a corporation's 12,000 voting shares with no attribution. The corporation redeems 4,000 of her shares, leaving her with 4,000 of 8,000. Is the redemption substantially disproportionate?
options: Yes, because 50 percent is less than 80 percent of her prior 66.67 percent
No, because she must own less than 50 percent of the voting power immediately afterwards, and exactly half fails
Yes, because she has reduced her holding by half
No, because the ratio test requires a reduction to under 20 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 302(b)(2) requires both limbs — the ratio test is met, since 50 percent is under 80 percent of 66.67 percent, but the limitation requires her to hold less than 50 percent of the voting power immediately after the redemption, and exactly half fails it.

questions.stem: Anselm holds 2 percent of a widely held corporation's voting stock with no attribution and no control. A redemption takes him to 1.7 percent, which is neither substantially disproportionate nor a complete termination. Which route to exchange treatment remains?
options: None; the redemption is a dividend under IRC § 301
IRC § 302(b)(1), if the redemption is not essentially equivalent to a dividend because it meaningfully reduces his proportionate interest
The IRC § 302(c)(2) waiver, filed with his return
IRC § 302(b)(2), because a minority holder is exempt from the ratio test
questions.explanation: IRC § 302(b)(1) is the fallback facts test, requiring a meaningful reduction in the shareholder's proportionate interest, and it works best for a small minority holder with no control to lose.

questions.stem: A distributor has adjusted taxable income of $900,000 for 2026, pays $300,000 of dividends, and is allowed an accumulated earnings credit of $200,000. Its accumulated earnings and profits at the close of 2025 were $5,000,000. On what amount is the accumulated earnings tax computed?
options: $5,000,000, the accumulated balance at the close of 2025
questions.explanation: IRC § 535(a) defines accumulated taxable income as the year's taxable income, adjusted, less the dividends paid deduction and less the accumulated earnings credit — $900,000 less $300,000 less $200,000; the accumulated balance is not the base.

questions.stem: On examination the Service establishes that a corporation accumulated earnings beyond the reasonable needs of its business. What is the effect on the question of purpose under IRC § 532(a)?
options: The Service must still separately prove a purpose to avoid shareholder tax
The accumulation is determinative of the purpose unless the corporation proves the contrary by a preponderance of the evidence
The purpose is conclusively established and cannot be rebutted
The accumulation is irrelevant unless the corporation is a mere holding company
questions.explanation: IRC § 533(a) makes accumulation beyond the reasonable needs of the business determinative of the purpose to avoid income tax unless the corporation proves the contrary by the preponderance of the evidence, so the corporation carries the burden of displacing it.

questions.stem: Two C corporations each have accumulated earnings and profits of $100,000 at the close of the preceding year and each retains $60,000 in the current year with no documented plan. One provides landscaping services; the other provides actuarial services. How do their minimum accumulated earnings credits compare?
options: They are equal, because both corporations are service businesses
The actuarial firm's is the smaller, because actuarial science is on the closed list of fields for which IRC § 535(c)(2) substitutes the lower statutory figure, and landscaping is not
The landscaper's is the smaller, because a service business outside the listed fields gets no minimum credit at all
Neither has a minimum credit, because $100,000 of accumulated earnings and profits exhausts it
questions.explanation: IRC § 535(c)(2)(B) substitutes a lower statutory figure only for a corporation whose principal function is performing services in one of the eight listed fields — actuarial science is on the closed list, landscaping is not — so the landscaper measures its minimum credit against the general figure and the actuarial firm against the lower one; both are the excess of the applicable figure over the same $100,000 balance.

questions.stem: A calendar-year corporation that is not a large corporation earns its income evenly through the year and expects 2026 tax of $200,000; its 2025 tax was $120,000. What is the smallest instalment it can pay on 15 April 2026 without an addition to tax?
questions.explanation: IRC § 6655(d)(1): each instalment is a quarter of the required annual payment, and the required annual payment is the lesser of this year's tax or last year's — a quarter of $120,000.

questions.stem: A corporation's 2024 taxable income was $1,200,000 before a net operating loss carryover and $700,000 after it. Its 2023 and 2025 taxable income were each under $400,000. Is it a large corporation for 2026?
options: No, because taxable income after the carryover was under a million
Yes, because the test is applied without regard to net operating loss carryovers
No, because the test requires a million in each of the three preceding years
Yes, but only if it is a member of a controlled group
questions.explanation: IRC § 6655(g)(2) makes a corporation large if it had taxable income of a million dollars or more in any of the three preceding years, computed without regard to net operating loss or capital loss carryovers; one year is enough.

questions.stem: A calendar-year corporation's controller was in hospital in December 2026 and the fourth instalment was paid three weeks late. What relief from the IRC § 6655(a) addition is available?
options: Full abatement for reasonable cause, as for a late return
None; the addition runs at the underpayment rate from 15 December until payment and has no reasonable cause defence
Abatement, provided the corporation is not a large corporation
Abatement, because the extended return date has not yet passed
questions.explanation: IRC § 6655(a) computes the addition at the IRC § 6621 underpayment rate on the shortfall for the period, making it an interest charge in substance; there is no reasonable cause defence as there is for a failure to file.

questions.stem: An applicable corporation pays $12,000,000 of corporate alternative minimum tax for 2026. Against what, and when, may the resulting credit be used?
options: Against the 2026 minimum tax itself, reducing the amount paid
Against regular tax in a later year in which regular tax exceeds tentative minimum tax
Against regular tax in 2026 only, with no carryforward
Against tentative minimum tax in the next year in which minimum tax is again owed
questions.explanation: IRC § 53(a) and (b) allow prior years' minimum tax as a credit against regular tax in a later year, limited by IRC § 53(c) to the excess of regular tax over tentative minimum tax and carried forward indefinitely; it does not reduce the minimum tax when paid.

questions.stem: An applicable corporation has a $50,000,000 minimum tax credit carryforward. This year its regular tax is $80,000,000, its tentative minimum tax is $75,000,000, and it owes $10,000,000 of base erosion tax. How much of the credit may it use?
options: Nil, because a base erosion tax suspends the credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 53(e)(2) increases the regular tax figure in the IRC § 53(c) limitation by the base erosion tax, so the room is $90,000,000 less $75,000,000; the remaining $35,000,000 carries forward under IRC § 53(b).

questions.stem: A corporation's taxable income has averaged $1,400,000,000 over the last three years, but its adjusted financial statement income has averaged $800,000,000 and has never crossed a billion in any period. Is it an applicable corporation?
options: Yes, because taxable income exceeds the billion-dollar threshold
Yes, because either measure over a billion suffices
No, because the test is measured on adjusted financial statement income under IRC § 56A, not taxable income
No, because the test looks only at the current year
questions.explanation: IRC § 59(k)(1) applies the average annual adjusted financial statement income test, and that income is computed under IRC § 56A — book income rather than taxable income — so a corporation under the threshold on book income is outside the regime whatever its taxable income.

questions.stem: A consultant receives shares worth $60,000 for services already performed, paying $10,000 for them. The shares are transferable immediately and not subject to any risk of forfeiture. What does she include, and when?
options: Nothing until the shares are sold
$50,000 of ordinary compensation income in the year of receipt
$60,000 of capital gain in the year of receipt
$50,000 of capital gain when the shares are sold
questions.explanation: IRC § 83(a) includes the value of the stock less anything paid for it as ordinary compensation income at the first moment the shares are transferable or not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, which here is immediately.
questions.pageTitle: Services rendered to a corporation in return for stock

questions.stem: A founder receives restricted stock worth $2,000 at formation, vesting over four years, and makes a timely IRC § 83(b) election. The stock is worth $500,000 when it fully vests. What does she include at vesting?
options: Nothing at vesting; she included $2,000 in the year of transfer
$2,000 at vesting
questions.explanation: IRC § 83(b) fixes the inclusion at the value on the date of transfer, disregarding restrictions that will lapse, so IRC § 83(a) does not apply at vesting and everything afterwards is capital appreciation on stock she already owns.
questions.pageTitle: Services rendered to a corporation in return for stock

questions.stem: Two property transferors receive 100 percent of a new corporation's issued shares. At the same time a key employee receives warrants over 30 percent of the fully diluted equity for agreeing to join. Do the property transferors have control?
options: No, because the warrants dilute them below 80 percent
Yes, because stock rights and warrants are not "stock" for the control computation
No, because the warrants are stock issued for services
Yes, but only if the warrants are never exercised
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.351-1(a)(1) excludes stock rights and stock warrants from the term "stock", so the warrants are not counted in the IRC § 368(c) computation and the transferors hold 100 percent of the stock that exists.
questions.pageTitle: Services rendered to a corporation in return for stock

questions.stem: Ines transfers land for 700 shares and Joaquin transfers equipment of substantial value for 300 shares, in a single planned transaction to a new corporation with no other stock. Does the exchange qualify for nonrecognition?
options: Neither transfer qualifies, because no single transferor holds 80 percent
Both qualify, because the property transferors are aggregated and together hold 100 percent immediately after the exchange
Only Ines qualifies, because Joaquin's 30 percent is below the control threshold
Both qualify only if each transferor separately holds at least 80 percent of a class
questions.explanation: IRC § 351(a) tests whether the transferors as a group are in control immediately after the exchange, and IRC § 368(c) is satisfied because several transferors acting together are aggregated.

questions.stem: A transferor contributes property with an aggregate basis of $1,000,000 and an aggregate fair market value of $700,000 to a controlled corporation, and the parties elect to reduce the transferor's stock basis rather than the corporation's basis. What are the two bases?
options: Corporation $700,000, stock $1,000,000
Corporation $1,000,000, stock $700,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 362(e)(2) caps the corporation's aggregate basis at fair market value where there is a net built-in loss, but the election reduces the transferor's stock basis instead and leaves the corporation with carryover basis, so the loss survives once.

questions.stem: In an exchange that otherwise qualifies, a transferor gives property worth $400,000 with a basis of $550,000 to a corporation she controls, receiving stock worth $340,000 and $60,000 of cash. What loss does she recognise?
options: $150,000, her full realised loss
$60,000, up to the cash received
Nothing: boot is a ceiling on gain, and no loss is recognised at all
$150,000, but only if the corporation elects to reduce its own basis instead
questions.explanation: IRC § 351(b)(2) provides that no loss is recognised, so receiving boot caps the gain that can be recognised but never unlocks a loss; the built-in loss stays in the bases, subject to the IRC § 362(e)(2) cap in the corporation's hands.

questions.stem: A transferor gives property worth $700,000 with a basis of $600,000 and receives stock worth $500,000 and $200,000 of cash in a qualifying exchange. What is the corporation's basis in the property?
questions.explanation: Gain recognised is $100,000, the lesser of the $100,000 realised gain and the $200,000 of boot under IRC § 351(b)(1); under IRC § 362(a) the corporation takes the $600,000 transferred basis increased by the gain recognised, not by the boot it paid.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer and/or receipt of money or property in addition to corporate stock

questions.stem: A transferor gives two assets: shares worth $600,000 with a basis of $200,000, and equipment worth $200,000 with a basis of $350,000. He receives stock worth $640,000 and $160,000 of cash. What gain is recognised?
options: Nothing, because the combined realised gain is offset by the loss
questions.explanation: The boot is allocated by relative fair market value, $120,000 to the shares and $40,000 to the equipment; the shares recognise $120,000 under IRC § 351(b)(1), and the equipment's realised loss produces nothing because IRC § 351(b)(2) recognises no loss.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer and/or receipt of money or property in addition to corporate stock

questions.stem: A transferor contributes inventory she has held for two years to a corporation in exchange for stock. What is the holding period of the stock?
options: It includes the two years
It begins afresh on the exchange
It includes the two years only if the corporation holds the inventory as a capital asset
It includes the two years, tacked under the corporation's holding period rule
questions.explanation: IRC § 1223(1) tacks the holding period only where the property exchanged was a capital asset or IRC § 1231 property in the transferor's hands, and inventory is neither.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer and/or receipt of money or property in addition to corporate stock

questions.stem: A transferor contributes two properties to a controlled corporation: a building with a basis of $100,000 subject to a $260,000 mortgage, and unencumbered land with a basis of $200,000. What gain arises under IRC § 357(c)?
options: $160,000, the excess of the mortgage over the basis of the building it encumbers
Nothing, because $260,000 does not exceed the $300,000 aggregate basis of all the property transferred
$260,000, the whole liability assumed
questions.explanation: IRC § 357(c)(1) compares the liabilities assumed with the total adjusted basis of the property transferred, so the two bases are aggregated and the mortgage does not exceed them.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer of property subject to indebtedness

questions.stem: A cash-basis proprietor incorporates, transferring receivables with a zero basis and equipment with a basis of $20,000, and the corporation assumes $35,000 of trade payables. What is her basis in the stock received?
options: Nil, because the payables exceed her basis and reduce it to zero
A negative basis of $15,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 358(d)(2) leaves out of the stock basis computation the same deductible liabilities that IRC § 357(c)(3) excludes, so the payables do not reduce her basis and it stays at the $20,000 she had in the equipment.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer of property subject to indebtedness

questions.stem: A transferor contributes a building worth $2,000,000 with a basis of $900,000, subject to a $600,000 mortgage taken out years ago for the business, to a corporation he will wholly own, receiving only stock. What is the consequence?
options: $600,000 of boot, with gain recognised up to that amount
The exchange fails because he received something other than stock
No gain: the assumed liability is not money or other property, and it does not exceed his basis
$300,000 of gain, the excess of his basis over the liability
questions.explanation: IRC § 357(a) provides that a liability assumed by the corporation is not treated as money or other property, so it produces no boot and does not disqualify the exchange; IRC § 357(c) is not triggered because $600,000 is below the $900,000 basis.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer of property subject to indebtedness

questions.stem: Holding corporation H owns 60 percent of the stock of each of corporations X and Y. No individual owns more than 10 percent of either. Do X and Y form a controlled group with H?
options: Yes, a brother-sister group, because H holds more than 50 percent of each identically
No: a corporation cannot be one of the five persons in the brother-sister test, and 60 percent is below the parent-subsidiary threshold
Yes, a combined group, because H is common to both
No, because a brother-sister group requires exactly equal percentages in each corporation
questions.explanation: IRC § 1563(a)(2) counts only persons who are individuals, estates or trusts, so a holding company is tested under the parent-subsidiary limb of IRC § 1563(a)(1), where 60 percent falls short of the 80 percent floor.

questions.stem: A calendar-year corporation joins a parent-subsidiary group on 12 February 2026 and is sold out of it on 20 November 2026. Is it a component member of the group for 2026?
options: Yes, because it was a member for more than half the days of the year
No, because membership is fixed on the 31 December included in the taxable year and it had left by then
Yes, for the nine months it was a member, on a pro rata basis
No, because a corporation must be a member for the entire year
questions.explanation: IRC § 1563(b)(1) fixes component membership on the 31 December included in the taxable year, so a corporation that left the group in November is not a member for that year.

questions.stem: A parent holds stock possessing 79 percent of a subsidiary's voting power and 79 percent of its value. Is the subsidiary in a parent-subsidiary controlled group?
options: Yes, because 79 percent rounds to the 80 percent threshold
Yes, because the two limbs together exceed 80 percent
No, because the test requires at least 80 percent of voting power or of value and neither limb reaches it
Yes, as a combined group under the insurance company rules
questions.explanation: IRC § 1563(a)(1) requires stock possessing at least 80 percent of the total combined voting power or at least 80 percent of the total value; eighty percent is a floor, and 79 percent is outside however close it looks.
