questions.stem: Four individuals hold stock carrying 70 percent of a C corporation's voting power but only 45 percent of its value; the remaining value is spread among hundreds of unrelated investors, none of whom holds more than 1 percent of it. Is the corporation closely held?
options: Yes, because four individuals hold more than half the voting power
No, because the test measures more than 50 percent in value and no five individuals reach that
Yes, because fewer than five individuals hold the voting stock
No, because a closely held corporation must have five or fewer shareholders in total
questions.explanation: IRC § 542(a)(2) asks whether more than 50 percent in value of the outstanding stock is owned by or for not more than 5 individuals; it measures value, not votes.

questions.stem: A closely held C corporation that is not a personal service corporation has a $300,000 loss from an activity covered by the at-risk rules, and is at risk for $120,000 at the close of the year. How much of the loss is allowed by the at-risk rules?
options: $300,000, because the at-risk rules do not apply to C corporations
$120,000, the amount at risk at the close of the year
$180,000, the excess of the loss over the amount at risk
Nothing, because a closely held C corporation may not deduct losses from covered activities
questions.explanation: IRC § 465(a)(1)(B) applies the at-risk limitation to a C corporation meeting the IRC § 542(a)(2) test, so the loss is allowed only up to the amount the corporation is at risk at the close of the year.

questions.stem: All of a C corporation's stock is held by three partnerships whose partners are, between them, four individuals. Its adviser says it cannot be closely held because no individual owns any stock directly. Is the adviser right?
options: Yes, because a partnership is not an individual and the five must own stock directly
No, because the stock is owned indirectly by or for the four individuals behind the partnerships
Yes, because stock held through entities is counted only in the first half of the year
No, but only if each partnership is itself a personal service corporation
questions.explanation: IRC § 542(a)(2) counts stock owned directly or indirectly by or for not more than 5 individuals, and the attribution rules look through a partnership shareholder to the individuals behind it.

questions.stem: Two shareholders hold identical shares of an S corporation issued under one certificate class. By settled practice, one takes $150,000 out of the corporation every year and the other takes nothing. What is the risk?
options: A second class of stock, because the outstanding shares do not in fact confer identical rights to distribution proceeds
None, because both hold shares of the same certificate class
None, because differences of this kind are disregarded under IRC § 1361(c)(4)
None, because the straight debt safe harbour applies
questions.explanation: IRC § 1361(b)(1)(D) turns on the rights the outstanding shares confer to distribution and liquidation proceeds, not on certificates, and a consistent pattern of disproportionate distributions is evidence the shares do not confer identical rights.

questions.stem: A shareholder dies and her stock passes under her will to a testamentary trust that is neither an electing small business trust nor a grantor trust. For how long may the trust hold the stock without terminating the election?
options: Two years beginning on the day the stock is transferred to it
Indefinitely
Not at all, because a trust is not a permitted shareholder
Until the estate is closed
questions.explanation: IRC § 1361(c)(2)(A) lists a testamentary trust among the trusts that may hold S corporation stock, but only for the two-year period beginning on the day the stock is transferred to it.

questions.stem: Which change causes an S corporation to become an ineligible corporation and lose its election?
options: Changing its business to that of an insurance company
Issuing non-voting common stock alongside voting common
Admitting a ninetieth individual shareholder
A deceased shareholder's estate continuing to hold shares
questions.explanation: IRC § 1361(b)(1) requires that the corporation not be an ineligible corporation, a defined term reaching certain financial institutions, insurance companies and DISCs; a corporation that moves its business into one of those categories loses its election.

questions.stem: A corporation made a valid S election in 2026 with every shareholder's consent. In 2027 an unrelated investor buys shares. Must the new shareholder consent to the election?
options: No, the election is the corporation's and continues without her consent
Yes, within two and a half months of acquiring the shares
Yes, or the election terminates on the date of the transfer
Yes, by filing an amended Form 2553
questions.explanation: IRC § 1362(a)(2) requires consent from all persons who are shareholders on the day the election is made; once a valid election exists, new shareholders need not consent to it.

questions.stem: Articles of incorporation are filed on 10 January. The corporation issues no shares, acquires no assets and conducts no business until 1 August. Form 2553 is filed on 1 March. The election is:
options: Invalid, because it was made before the first taxable year began
Valid for the first taxable year
Valid, but effective for the following taxable year
Valid if the corporation shows reasonable cause
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.1362-6(a)(2)(ii): a new corporation's taxable year begins when it first has shareholders, acquires assets or begins doing business, and the existence of incorporators does not begin it; an election made before that date is made in neither the preceding year nor the effective year.

questions.stem: A new corporation's first taxable year runs from 1 November to 31 December. It files Form 2553 on 10 January of the following year. Is the election effective for that first short year?
options: Yes, because for a year of two and a half months or less an election made before the sixteenth day of the third month after the first day of the year is treated as made during that year
No, because the taxable year had already ended
No, because the deadline was 15 December
No, it is treated as made for the following taxable year
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.1362-6(a)(2)(ii)(A): where the first taxable year is 2½ months or less, an election made before the sixteenth day of the third month after the first day of that year — here 16 January — is treated as made during it.

questions.stem: Which of the following items of an S corporation is folded into nonseparately computed income rather than stated separately?
options: Wages paid to employees
A long-term capital gain on an investment parcel
A cash gift to a public charity
Interest on a state bond
questions.explanation: IRC § 1366(a)(2) defines nonseparately computed income as gross income less deductions allowed, excluding every item whose separate treatment could affect a shareholder's liability; wages meet no shareholder-level rate, limit or character rule, while the other three do.
questions.pageTitle: Income, expenses and separately stated items

questions.stem: An S corporation with five equal shareholders redeems one shareholder's entire holding on 1 July and wants to close the books under IRC § 1377(a)(2). Whose agreement is required?
options: The corporation and all five shareholders
The corporation and the departing shareholder only
The departing shareholder and the four remaining shareholders, but not the corporation
Shareholders holding a majority of the shares
questions.explanation: IRC § 1377(a)(2)(B): where the transfer is to the corporation itself, every person who is a shareholder during the taxable year is an affected shareholder, and IRC § 1377(a)(2)(A) requires the agreement of the corporation as well.
questions.pageTitle: Income, expenses and separately stated items

questions.stem: A shareholder owning 10 percent of an S corporation sells all her shares on 15 January and stays on as an employee. The corporation pays her health premiums for the rest of the year. Is she a 2-percent shareholder for that year?
options: Yes, because ownership is tested on any day during the taxable year
No, because she owned no stock when the premiums were paid
No, because ownership is tested at the end of the year
Only if stock is attributed to her under IRC § 318
questions.explanation: IRC § 1372(b) defines a 2-percent shareholder as a person owning more than 2 percent of the stock on any day during the taxable year, so a sale in January does not undo the status for that year.
questions.pageTitle: Income, expenses and separately stated items

questions.stem: Marlow Optics Inc. has been an S corporation since it was organised and has never acquired a C corporation. Its sole shareholder's stock basis is $110,000 at the start of the year; the corporation earns $40,000 of ordinary income and distributes $140,000 in December. How is the distribution characterised?
options: $110,000 is a recovery of basis and $30,000 is gain from the sale or exchange of property
$110,000 is a recovery of basis and $30,000 is a dividend
The whole $140,000 is a tax-free recovery of basis, because basis is first increased by the year's income
The whole $140,000 is a dividend to the extent of the accumulated adjustments account
questions.explanation: IRC § 1368(d) directs that basis is increased for the year's income before the distribution is measured, taking it to $150,000; with no accumulated earnings and profits under IRC § 1371(c), IRC § 1368(b) makes the whole $140,000 a recovery of basis, leaving $10,000, with no gain and no dividend.

questions.stem: An S corporation with accumulated earnings and profits has an accumulated adjustments account of $30,000 at the close of the year. It distributed $20,000 in February and $80,000 in October. How much of the October distribution is treated under IRC § 1368(b)?
options: Nothing, because the February distribution used the account first
questions.explanation: IRC § 1368(c), flush text: where distributions exceed the account, its balance is allocated among them in proportion to their sizes — 20 to 80 — so $6,000 goes to February and $24,000 to October, with the rest of each a dividend to the extent of the accumulated earnings and profits.

questions.stem: An S corporation with $100,000 of accumulated earnings and profits begins the year with an accumulated adjustments account of $50,000. It has no income, losses or deductions for the year and distributes $70,000. What is the account balance at the close of the year?
options: Negative $20,000
Negative $70,000
Zero
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.1368-2(a)(3)(ii), (iii): losses may take the account below zero but a distribution may not, so the account stops at zero and the $20,000 excess is a dividend under IRC § 1368(c)(2).

questions.stem: A shareholder begins the year with stock basis of $20,000. The S corporation reports $30,000 of ordinary income, $12,000 of non-deductible fines, a $45,000 ordinary loss, and distributes $25,000 to her. No election under Reg. § 1.1367-1(g) is made. How much of the loss may she deduct this year?
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.1367-1(f): income first takes basis to $50,000, the distribution next to $25,000, the non-deductible fines third to $13,000, and the loss comes last — so $13,000 is allowed and $32,000 is suspended under IRC § 1366(d)(1).

questions.stem: A shareholder holds a $50,000 written note from the S corporation. Losses in earlier years reduced his stock basis to zero and the note's basis to $20,000. This year the corporation has a net increase of $18,000 and repays the note in full. What does he recognise on the repayment?
options: $30,000 of gain
No gain
$32,000 of gain
$12,000 of gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 1367(b)(2)(B): the net increase restores the basis of the indebtedness before any of it reaches stock, so the note's basis rises from $20,000 to $38,000 and a $50,000 repayment against a $38,000 basis produces $12,000 of gain.

questions.stem: An S corporation earns $10,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest during the year. What effect does that income have on the shareholder's stock basis and on the corporation's accumulated adjustments account?
options: It increases both by $10,000
It increases neither, because it is not taxable
It increases stock basis but not the accumulated adjustments account
It increases the accumulated adjustments account but not stock basis
questions.explanation: IRC § 1367(a)(1)(A) reaches the IRC § 1366(a)(1)(A) items, which expressly include tax-exempt income, while IRC § 1368(e)(1)(A) excludes it from the account — two accounts, two answers.

questions.stem: A calendar-year S corporation files a revocation on 10 March 2026 with the consent of holders of 60 percent of its shares. The revocation specifies no effective date. It takes effect on:
options: 1 January 2026
1 January 2027
10 March 2026
1 April 2026
questions.explanation: IRC § 1362(d)(1)(C)(i): a revocation made on or before the fifteenth day of the third month of the taxable year is effective on the first day of that year, retroactively across the weeks already operated as an S corporation.

questions.stem: An S corporation's election terminates on 1 June 2026, giving an S short year from 1 January to 31 May. When is the return for the S short year due?
options: On the same date as the return for the C short year, including extensions
15 March 2027, the ordinary Form 1120-S date
The fifteenth day of the third month after 31 May
Within 45 days of the termination
questions.explanation: IRC § 1362(e)(6)(B): the return for the S short year is due on the same date as the return for the C short year, including extensions, so the S short year return is pulled to the C corporation's date.

questions.stem: A calendar-year S corporation with accumulated earnings and profits at the close of each year has passive investment income above the threshold in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Its election terminates on:
options: 1 January 2027
31 December 2026
1 January 2025
The day in 2026 on which passive receipts first exceeded the threshold
questions.explanation: IRC § 1362(d)(3)(A): where both limbs are met for three consecutive taxable years, the termination is effective on the first day of the taxable year beginning after the third such year.

questions.stem: A solvent S corporation outside bankruptcy has $60,000 of debt forgiven by a supplier. Its sole shareholder has stock basis of $10,000 and $40,000 of suspended losses. What is the result?
options: $60,000 passes through as income, stock basis rises to $70,000 and the whole $40,000 of suspended losses is freed
$60,000 is excluded and the suspended losses are reduced to nil
$60,000 passes through but does not increase stock basis
Nothing passes through, because discharge income stays at the corporation
questions.explanation: IRC § 1366(a)(1)(B) passes the included discharge income through as ordinary income and IRC § 1367(a)(1)(B) increases stock basis by it; no exclusion applies to a solvent corporation, so IRC § 108(b) attribute reduction never arises.

questions.stem: Immediately before a lender forgives a $200,000 note, an S corporation has assets worth $500,000 and liabilities of $650,000 including that note. By how much is it insolvent for IRC § 108(a)(1)(B)?
options: Nothing, because after the discharge liabilities are less than assets
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(d)(3) measures insolvency as the excess of liabilities over the fair market value of assets immediately before the discharge, so the note about to be forgiven is still counted: $650,000 less $500,000.

questions.stem: Under current law, an amount of discharge income that an S corporation excludes under IRC § 108(a):
options: Is not taken into account under IRC § 1366(a) and does not increase stock basis
Passes through as tax-exempt income and increases stock basis
Increases stock basis, but only after the attribute reduction
Passes through as ordinary income to the shareholders
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(d)(7)(A), as amended by Pub. L. 107-147 § 402(a) to reverse Gitlitz v. Commissioner, applies the exclusion at the corporate level including by not taking the excluded amount into account under IRC § 1366(a).

questions.stem: An S corporation distributes a building worth $400,000, subject to a $250,000 mortgage that the shareholder takes subject to. The shareholder's basis in the building is:
options: The corporation's adjusted basis in the building
questions.explanation: IRC § 301(d) gives the shareholder a basis equal to the property's full fair market value; the liability reduces the amount of the distribution under IRC § 301(b)(2) but not the basis, because the shareholder has taken on the debt.

questions.stem: An S corporation with no accumulated earnings and profits distributes property worth $300,000 with an adjusted basis of $100,000 to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $150,000. What does she report?
options: $200,000 of pass-through gain and no gain under IRC § 1368(b)(2)
$200,000 of pass-through gain plus $150,000 under IRC § 1368(b)(2)
$150,000 under IRC § 1368(b)(2) only
Nothing, because the distribution is a return of basis
questions.explanation: IRC § 311(b)(1) treats the property as sold at $300,000, and the $200,000 gain passes through and raises her stock basis to $350,000 under IRC § 1367(a)(1) before the distribution is measured; the $300,000 distribution is then within basis under IRC § 1368(b).

questions.stem: A corporation that converted from C to S status four years ago, still inside its recognition period, distributes land carrying unrecognised built-in gain. Beyond the pass-through of the IRC § 311(b)(1) gain, what follows?
options: A corporate-level built-in gains tax under IRC § 1374, fed back to the shareholders as a loss under IRC § 1366(f)(2)
Nothing further, because an S corporation pays no entity-level tax
The built-in gain is deferred until the shareholder sells the land
The distribution is a dividend to the extent of the built-in gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 1374 converts a deemed sale within the recognition period into a recognised built-in gain subject to entity-level tax, and IRC § 1366(f)(2) treats that tax as a loss of the corporation so shareholders bear it once.

questions.stem: A newly formed corporation's first taxable year runs for four months, during which it has $6,000,000 of gross receipts. For the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test, what figure is used for that year?
options: The year is ignored because it is short
questions.explanation: IRC § 448(c)(3) annualises a short taxable year by multiplying gross receipts by 12 and dividing by the number of months — $6,000,000 times 12 over 4.

questions.stem: An accrual method business receives $30,000 in December 2026 for services it will perform entirely in 2027. It has made no election under IRC § 451(c). In which year is the $30,000 income?
options: All of it in 2026, the year of receipt
All of it in 2027, when the services are performed
Ratably as the services are performed
Half in each year
questions.explanation: IRC § 451(c)(1)(A): without the election, an accrual method taxpayer includes an advance payment in gross income in the year of receipt; only the election under IRC § 451(c)(1)(B) defers any portion, and then only to the following year.

questions.stem: In 2026 a sole proprietor is paid $9,000 through a third party settlement organisation across 45 transactions. Will she receive a Form 1099-K, and is the $9,000 income?
options: She will receive the form, and the amount is income
She will not receive the form because neither the dollar nor the transaction test is met, but the $9,000 is income regardless
She will not receive the form, so the amount is not income
She will receive the form because the lower flat-dollar threshold enacted in 2021 still applies
questions.explanation: IRC § 6050W(e) as restored by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70432(a) requires both the dollar and the transaction-count tests to be exceeded, and the 2021 reduction is treated as never having taken effect; whether a form issues is the payer's obligation and says nothing about her gross income under IRC § 61(a).

questions.stem: Farleigh Parts Inc. begins the year with no inventory and buys 100 units at $10 in January, 100 at $12 in June and 100 at $14 in October. It has 150 units on hand at the year end. Under FIFO, what is its cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: Under FIFO the earliest goods are sold first, so the 150 units on hand carry the latest costs — 100 at $14 plus 50 at $12, or $2,000 of ending inventory — and cost of goods sold is $3,600 of purchases less $2,000. With prices rising, LIFO would give $2,000 and average cost $1,800, and the figure reduces gross income under Reg. § 1.61-3(a) rather than being claimed as a deduction.

questions.stem: A wholesaler whose average annual gross receipts are well below the IRC § 448(c) figure for 2026 chooses not to maintain an inventory under IRC § 471(a). How may it account for its stock?
options: As non-incidental materials and supplies, or by conforming to the method in its applicable financial statement or, having none, its books and records
By deducting every purchase when paid, whether or not the goods are sold
It must still choose between FIFO and LIFO
It must capitalise its purchasing and storage costs under IRC § 263A
questions.explanation: IRC § 471(c)(1)(B) gives a small business taxpayer those two alternatives, and the same IRC § 448(c) test takes it outside IRC § 263A under IRC § 263A(i), so it has neither obligation.

questions.stem: A manufacturer subject to IRC § 263A spends $200,000 on domestic research to improve a product it holds in inventory and deducts the amount under IRC § 174A. Must the $200,000 be capitalised into the cost of the inventory?
options: Yes, because every cost tied to production is capitalised under IRC § 263A
No, because amounts allowable as a deduction under IRC § 174 or § 174A are excluded from capitalisation
Yes, but only the portion allocable to units still on hand at the year end
No, because research costs are never allowable as a deduction
questions.explanation: IRC § 263A(c)(2) excludes any amount allowable as a deduction under section 174 or 174A from capitalisation under the section, so the research stays a current deduction while the ordinary production costs are capitalised.

questions.stem: Ferrers, who is single with $150,000 of wages and no other business, has a $90,000 share of loss from a non-rental partnership in which he materially participates. His outside basis and his at-risk amount are each $200,000, all from cash he contributed. How much of the loss reduces his 2026 taxable income?
options: Nothing, because wages are excluded from the excess business loss computation
Nothing, because a partnership loss is passive unless the partner is a general partner
$90,000, but only against future partnership income
questions.explanation: IRC § 461(l)(3)(A): the loss clears basis under IRC § 704(d), at-risk under IRC § 465(a)(1) and passive under IRC § 469 because he materially participates, and $90,000 is well below the single-filer threshold in Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 3.31; wages are left out of the computation, but the allowed loss still offsets them.
questions.pageTitle: Net income, net operating losses, and loss limitations

questions.stem: A couple filing jointly for 2026 have a $700,000 loss from a manufacturing business, a $30,000 loss from selling stock, and $450,000 of wages. Both are fully at risk and materially participate. What is the excess business loss?
options: Nothing, because the wages absorb the loss
questions.explanation: IRC § 461(l)(3)(B) leaves capital losses out of the deduction side and IRC § 461(l)(3)(A) leaves wages out entirely, so only the $700,000 business loss is measured against the joint threshold, and the $188,000 above it becomes a net operating loss under IRC § 461(l)(2).
questions.pageTitle: Net income, net operating losses, and loss limitations

questions.stem: A sole proprietor's 2026 loss survives all four limitations and becomes a net operating loss. Which statement about using it in other years is correct?
options: It may be carried back two years whatever the business, then forward twenty years
It carries forward indefinitely with no carryback, unless it is a farming loss, which alone keeps a carryback
It carries forward twenty years without any percentage cap
It may be carried back five years under the 2020 relief
questions.explanation: IRC § 172(b)(1)(A)(ii) gives an indefinite carryforward with no general carryback, and the only carryback left is the two-year farming loss carryback under IRC § 172(b)(1)(B)(i); the twenty-year rule belongs to pre-2018 losses and the five-year carryback to 2018 through 2020 losses only.
questions.pageTitle: Net income, net operating losses, and loss limitations

questions.stem: Wetheral Tooling Ltd is not in bankruptcy. Immediately before a lender discharges $200,000 of a working-capital loan, its liabilities exceed the fair market value of its assets by $120,000. None of the debt is farm or real property business indebtedness. What does the company report?
options: Nothing, because the whole $200,000 is excluded
$80,000 of ordinary income, with $120,000 excluded
$200,000 of ordinary income, because it is not in a title 11 case
$120,000 of ordinary income, with $80,000 excluded
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(a)(3) and IRC § 108(d)(3): the insolvency exclusion cannot exceed the amount of the insolvency, measured immediately before the discharge, so $120,000 is excluded and the remaining $80,000 is income under IRC § 61(a)(11).

questions.stem: A solvent corporation owes a bank $500,000 on a note. Its controlling shareholder, a person related to the corporation for this purpose, buys the note from the bank for $350,000. What is the result for the corporation?
options: No income, because the debt remains outstanding and is now owed to the shareholder
$150,000 of discharge of indebtedness income
$150,000 of income to the shareholder rather than the corporation
$350,000 of discharge of indebtedness income
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(e)(4)(A) treats the acquisition of the debt by a related person as an acquisition by the debtor, which produces discharge income to the extent of the discount — buying your own debt through a relative does not work.

questions.stem: A partnership is insolvent, but each of its partners is solvent. A lender discharges $300,000 of the partnership's debt. Whose insolvency is tested for the exclusion?
options: The partnership's, because it is the debtor
Each partner's, because the exclusion is applied at the partner level
Neither, because a partnership cannot use the insolvency exclusion
The partners', but only if the partnership elects
questions.explanation: IRC § 108(d)(6) applies the exclusions at the partner level, the opposite of the corporate-level rule in IRC § 108(d)(7)(A), so it is each partner's own balance sheet that decides whether anything is excluded.

questions.stem: In its taxable year beginning 1 January 2026, a publicly held corporation pays $3,000,000 to its top salesperson, who is not an officer. Is the deduction limited by the cap on excessive employee remuneration?
options: Yes, because she is among the five highest compensated employees
No, because for a taxable year beginning in 2026 only the principal executive officer, the principal financial officer and the three highest compensated officers are covered employees
Yes, because the cap reaches every employee of a publicly held corporation
No, because sales commissions are performance-based compensation
questions.explanation: IRC § 162(m)(3): the five highest compensated employees other than the covered officers are added only for taxable years beginning after 31 December 2026, so in 2026 her pay sits outside the cap entirely. The performance-based exclusion ended for taxable years beginning after 2017.

questions.stem: Pemberton owns 30 percent of the stock of an S corporation and works in it full time. The corporation pays $9,000 of health insurance premiums for him. How is the premium treated?
options: Deductible by the corporation and excluded from his income under IRC § 106(a)
Deductible by the corporation as compensation and included in his income
Not deductible by the corporation
Excluded from his income only if he owns more than 50 percent of the stock
questions.explanation: IRC § 1372(a) treats an S corporation as a partnership for fringe benefit purposes and a more-than-2-percent shareholder under IRC § 1372(b) as a partner, and a partner is never an employee for this rule; the corporation still deducts the cost, but as compensation to him.

questions.stem: An accrual method calendar-year C corporation accrues a $60,000 bonus on 31 December 2026 to its cash method vice-president, who owns 40 percent of its stock with no attribution from anyone else. The bonus is paid on 10 March 2027. The corporation is not a personal service corporation. When is the bonus deductible?
options: 2027, because the payee is a cash method shareholder
2026, because a 40 percent shareholder without attribution is not a related person
2027, because every bonus accrued to a shareholder is deferred until paid
Never, because the payment is a disguised dividend
questions.explanation: IRC § 267(b)(2) requires more than 50 percent ownership before the matching rule of IRC § 267(a)(2) applies, so the parties are not related and the ordinary accrual rules allow the deduction in 2026 while she reports in 2027 — a one-year mismatch the statute permits.

questions.stem: Pemberton owns a warehouse and leases it to a distribution partnership in which she holds a 10 percent interest but does no work. The lease produces $15,000 of net rental income and she has $15,000 of suspended passive losses from another property. How much of the losses can she use?
options: None, because the rental income is recharacterised as non-passive
All $15,000, because she does not materially participate in the tenant's business so the income stays passive
$1,500, in proportion to her 10 percent interest
All $15,000, but only if the tenant is a C corporation
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.469-2(f)(6) applies only where the taxpayer materially participates in the trade or business activity the property is rented for use in; she does not, so the income stays passive under IRC § 469(c)(2) and absorbs the suspended losses.

questions.stem: An accrual method corporation accrues $24,000 of rent owed to its sole shareholder, a cash method individual, on 31 December 2026 and pays it on 15 March 2027. In which year does the corporation deduct the rent?
options: 2026, when it was accrued
2027, when the shareholder includes it in income
2026, because it was paid within two and a half months of year end
Neither year, because rent paid to a related party is not deductible
questions.explanation: IRC § 267(a)(2) matches the deduction to the related cash method payee's inclusion, and it speaks of "expenses and interest" without limiting the kind of expense, so rent is caught just as an accrued bonus would be.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's self-rental loss is fully absorbed by passive income from an unrelated activity, so IRC § 469 does not suspend it. Which limitation can still stop the loss?
options: None, because clearing the passive activity rules is the final test
The excess business loss limitation of IRC § 461(l), which is applied after IRC § 469
The matching rule of IRC § 267(a)(2)
The employer rental rule of IRC § 280A(c)(6)
questions.explanation: IRC § 461(l) became permanent in July 2025, and a self-rental loss that escapes IRC § 469 in a year with passive income then joins the aggregate that IRC § 461(l) tests; the two limitations are sequential.

questions.stem: Fenwick Tools spends $30,000 of start-up expenditure and begins its active business on 1 July 2026. What is its total 2026 deduction under IRC § 195?
questions.explanation: IRC § 195(b)(1)(A) allows $5,000 in the opening year because the expenditure does not exceed $50,000, and IRC § 195(b)(1)(B) amortises the remaining $25,000 over 180 months from July, giving six months' worth, about $833, in 2026.
questions.pageTitle: Depreciation, amortization, IRC Section 179, depletion and bonus depreciation

questions.stem: A manufacturer places several five-year assets in service in 2026 and elects out of bonus depreciation for that class. Which statement is correct?
options: The election covers every five-year asset placed in service that year and can be revoked only with IRS consent
The election is made asset by asset, so one machine can be excluded and the rest kept
The election can be made on an amended return at any time within three years
The election lapses automatically at the end of the year and must be renewed
questions.explanation: IRC § 168(k)(7) lets a taxpayer elect out for a class of property by a statement attached to a timely filed return, including extensions, for the placed-in-service year; the election applies to every asset in that class placed in service that year and is revocable only with IRS consent.
questions.pageTitle: Depreciation, amortization, IRC Section 179, depletion and bonus depreciation

questions.stem: A uranium mine computes percentage depletion at the 22 percent rate as $22,000 for the year, but its cost depletion on the same property is $30,000. What is its depletion allowance?
options: $22,000, because percentage depletion replaces cost depletion
$30,000, because the allowance can never be less than cost depletion
$52,000, because both methods are allowed
Nothing, because uranium is not a listed mineral
questions.explanation: IRC § 613(a) closes by providing that the allowance shall in no case be less than it would be computed without reference to that section, so percentage depletion is floored by cost depletion.
questions.pageTitle: Depreciation, amortization, IRC Section 179, depletion and bonus depreciation

questions.stem: A corporation lends $60,000 to an unrelated start-up as a side investment with no connection to its own operations. The loan becomes wholly worthless in 2026. How is the loss treated?
options: As a short-term capital loss under the non-business bad debt rule
As an ordinary deduction, because a corporation cannot have a non-business bad debt
As a long-term capital loss, because the loan was outstanding more than a year
No deduction, because the loss bears no proximate relation to the corporation's business
questions.explanation: IRC § 166(d)(1) opens "In the case of a taxpayer other than a corporation," so every debt a corporation holds is within IRC § 166(a) and the business or non-business classification never arises.

questions.stem: An accrual method business is owed $50,000 by a bankrupt customer. In 2026 it charges off $35,000 on its books and deducts that amount. In 2028 the estate distributes $25,000 and closes. What is the 2028 consequence?
options: $10,000 is included in 2028 income, to the extent the 2026 deduction produced a tax benefit
The whole $25,000 is included in 2028 income
The 2026 return is amended to reduce the deduction to $25,000
Nothing, because a recovery of a bad debt is never income
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.166-1(f) treats a recovery of an amount previously deducted as income in the year received; the first $15,000 clears the unwritten balance and the $10,000 above it is a recovery, taxable only so far as the earlier deduction gave a tax benefit under IRC § 111.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor advances $30,000 to her brother with no note, no interest and no repayment date. Two years later he says he cannot repay. What may she deduct?
options: A short-term capital loss as a non-business bad debt
An ordinary deduction, if the advance related to her business
Nothing, because there was never a bona fide debt
Nothing this year, but a deduction once the brother is formally bankrupt
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.166-1(c) requires a genuine debtor-creditor relationship founded on a valid and enforceable obligation to repay a fixed sum; an advance with no note, no interest and no repayment terms is a gift when made, so there is no bad debt to deduct under either IRC § 166(a) or IRC § 166(d).

questions.stem: A firm hosts a client dinner that is lavish and extravagant in the circumstances, at $900 a head. An employee of the firm attends throughout. What may the firm deduct?
options: 50 percent of the cost
100 percent, because the meal was provided by a restaurant
Nothing, because a lavish meal fails the conditions that apply before any halving
$25 per client, as a gift
questions.explanation: IRC § 274(k)(1) requires that the food or beverages not be lavish or extravagant and that the taxpayer or an employee be present, and only a meal that clears both conditions is then halved by IRC § 274(n)(1); a lavish meal is not deducted at half, it is not deducted at all.
questions.pageTitle: Business travel, meals, and gift expenses

questions.stem: A firm distributes 500 identical wall calendars, each costing it $3.50 and permanently imprinted with its name, to customers and prospects. How much of the $1,750 is deductible?
options: $25 per recipient
All $1,750, because the calendars are not gifts for this purpose
Nothing, because they are entertainment
50 percent, because promotional items are treated like meals
questions.explanation: IRC § 274(b)(1)(A) takes an item costing not more than $4.00, clearly and permanently imprinted with the taxpayer's name and one of a number of identical items distributed generally, outside the gift limit entirely.
questions.pageTitle: Business travel, meals, and gift expenses

questions.stem: In 2026 a consultant takes a client to a restaurant for a $200 business meal. It is not lavish and she is present. What may she deduct?
options: $200, because restaurant meals are fully deductible
$100, because the full deduction for restaurant meals applied only to 2021 and 2022
Nothing, because meals with clients are entertainment
$25, because the meal is a gift to the client
questions.explanation: IRC § 274(n)(2)(D), added by Pub. L. 116-260 § 210(a), lifted the haircut only for amounts paid or incurred after 31 December 2020 and before 1 January 2023, so in 2026 the ordinary halving under IRC § 274(n)(1) applies.
questions.pageTitle: Business travel, meals, and gift expenses

questions.stem: A sole proprietor uses the standard mileage rate for her car. In 2026 she also pays $600 of parking and tolls on business calls, $900 as the business share of interest on the loan that bought the car, and $2,100 of insurance. What may she deduct in addition to the mileage?
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.274-5(j)(2): the rate stands in lieu of the actual costs of operating the vehicle, and insurance is one of those costs. Parking, tolls and the business portion of loan interest for a taxpayer other than an employee are outside the rate and remain deductible.

questions.stem: A company places two identical passenger automobiles in service in 2026, one for which the IRC § 168(k) additional first year depreciation deduction applies and one for which it does not. How do the IRC § 280F(a) limitation tables for the two cars differ?
options: In every year, in proportion to the bonus percentage
Only in the first year, by a fixed statutory amount
Not at all, because the caps are set by the year placed in service
Only in the years after the third
questions.explanation: Rev. Proc. 2026-15 Tables 1 and 2 differ only in the first taxable year, and the whole gap is the fixed amount by which IRC § 168(k)(2)(F)(i) increases the first-year limitation; the second, third and later-year figures are identical.

questions.stem: A consulting firm buys a $95,000 sport utility vehicle rated above the weight threshold that takes it outside the definition of a passenger automobile, places it in service in 2026 with 100 percent business use, and elects to expense it in full under IRC § 179. What is the result?
options: The full $95,000 is expensed, because the vehicle is not a passenger automobile
The expensing is limited by the passenger automobile caps in IRC § 280F(a)
The expensing is limited by the separate IRC § 179 ceiling for sport utility vehicles, and the rest is recovered through ordinary depreciation
Nothing may be expensed, because a vehicle is listed property
questions.explanation: IRC § 179(b)(5)(A) caps the cost of a sport utility vehicle that may be taken into account under IRC § 179; escaping the IRC § 280F(a) caps built for cars does not escape the ceiling Congress built for sport utility vehicles.

questions.stem: Marlow borrows $40,000 secured by a mortgage on her personal residence and spends the entire proceeds on inventory for her retail business. The interest on the loan is:
options: Personal interest, because the loan is secured by her home
Business interest, because the proceeds were spent on a business expenditure
Deductible only if the loan documents describe it as a business loan
Split evenly between business and personal use
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.163-8T(a)(3), (c)(1): interest is allocated by tracing the disbursement of the proceeds to the expenditure, and what secures the debt is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Thornbury Castings fails the IRC § 448(c) test. For 2026 it has business interest expense of $4,000,000, business interest income of $100,000, no floor plan financing interest, and adjusted taxable income of $10,000,000. How much business interest may it deduct?
questions.explanation: IRC § 163(j)(1): the limitation is the sum of business interest income, the statutory share of adjusted taxable income and floor plan financing interest — $100,000 plus $3,000,000. The $900,000 excess carries forward under IRC § 163(j)(2); $5,100,000 would apply the higher pandemic-year share that IRC § 163(j)(10) confined to 2019 and 2020.

questions.stem: Kestrel Freight LP, a partnership above the IRC § 448(c) threshold, has business interest expense exceeding its limitation for 2026, and one of its partners separately has an excess business loss. At which level is each limitation applied?
options: Both at the partner level
Both at the partnership level
IRC § 163(j) at the partnership level and IRC § 461(l) at the partner level
IRC § 163(j) at the partner level and IRC § 461(l) at the partnership level
questions.explanation: IRC § 163(j)(4)(A) applies the interest limitation at the partnership level, whereas the excess business loss rule in IRC § 461(l)(4) runs at the partner; the two sit next to each other in the same computation and apply at different levels.

questions.stem: A corporation takes out a policy on its owner's life and assigns it to its bank as collateral for a loan, so the bank rather than the corporation would receive the proceeds. Are the premiums deductible?
options: Yes, because the bank rather than the corporation is the beneficiary
No, because the corporation is indirectly a beneficiary under the policy
Yes, as interest on the loan the policy secures
Yes, provided the owner consented in writing before issue
questions.explanation: IRC § 264(a)(1) denies the deduction where the taxpayer is "directly or indirectly a beneficiary," which reaches a policy the business assigns to a lender as collateral, not only one payable to the company outright.

questions.stem: On 1 November 2026 a cash method business pays a $24,000 premium for twelve months of liability cover running from 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2028. When is it deductible?
options: In full in 2026, because the cover lasts only twelve months
Spread over the policy term, because the benefit ends after the close of 2027
In full in 2027, when the cover begins
Half in 2026 and half in 2027
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.263(a)-4(f)(1) has two limbs, twelve months from first realisation and the end of the taxable year following payment; the cover ends in 2028, after the close of 2027, so the second limb fails and the premium must be spread.

questions.stem: A corporation holds a key-person policy on its founder issued in 2003 with no notice or consent, having paid $90,000 of premiums. It receives $800,000 on her death in 2026. How much does it include in income?
options: Nothing
questions.explanation: IRC § 101(j) and IRC § 6039I apply only to contracts issued after 17 August 2006, so an older key-person policy is outside both and the death benefit is fully excluded under IRC § 101(a)(1) with no notice and consent condition.

questions.stem: A corporation pays $50,000 of income tax to a foreign country and claims the IRC § 901 credit for $30,000 of it. May it deduct the remaining $20,000?
options: Yes, the portion not credited may be deducted under IRC § 164
No, because the deduction is denied once the taxpayer chooses the credit to any extent
Yes, but only as an itemized deduction
No, because foreign income taxes are never deductible
questions.explanation: IRC § 275(a)(4) denies the deduction for a foreign income tax where the taxpayer chooses the IRC § 901 credit "to any extent," so a foreign income tax is deductible or creditable, not both.

questions.stem: A retailer with average annual gross receipts of $20,000,000 for the testing period pays $12,000 of sales tax on goods it buys for resale in 2026. How is the tax treated?
options: Capitalised into inventory and recovered through cost of goods sold
Deducted in the year paid as a tax paid in carrying on a trade or business
Capitalised as part of a depreciable asset
Not deductible at all
questions.explanation: IRC § 263A(i) exempts a business that meets the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test from capitalising the tax into inventory, so it is deducted under the business catch-all in the flush text of IRC § 164(a). Above the threshold the identical tax would be capitalised under IRC § 263A(a)(2)(B).

questions.stem: A company settles a state enforcement action. The signed agreement identifies $300,000 of the payment as reimbursement of the agency's costs of investigating the matter. Is that $300,000 deductible?
options: Yes, because the agreement identifies the amount and it is not a penalty
No, because reimbursement of a government's investigation costs is outside the restitution exception
Yes, as an ordinary and necessary business expense under IRC § 162(a)
Yes, if the company can show the investigation found no violation
questions.explanation: IRC § 162(f)(2)(B) provides that amounts paid as reimbursement of the government's investigation or litigation costs are not restitution or compliance payments, so the exception in IRC § 162(f)(2)(A) never reaches them whatever the agreement says.

questions.stem: An employer has ten employees, each paid well above the FUTA wage base, in a state whose unemployment fund is in good standing, and it paid its state contributions on time. What is its net federal unemployment tax for 2026?
questions.explanation: IRC § 3301 imposes the tax at the statutory rate on FUTA wages, ten times the IRC § 3306(b)(1) base or $70,000, and the IRC § 3302(a), (b) credits for timely state contributions bring the net rate down to 0.6 percent, or $420.

questions.stem: A married employee who files jointly earns $230,000 in 2026 from a single employer. How much additional hospital insurance tax must the employer withhold?
options: Nothing, because the joint-return threshold has not been reached
0.9 percent of $30,000, because the employer withholds once wages from it exceed $200,000 regardless of filing status
0.9 percent of $230,000
1.45 percent of $30,000, matched by the employer
questions.explanation: IRC § 3101(b)(2) sets thresholds by filing status, which the employer does not know, so the employer withholds once wages from that employer alone exceed the single threshold and any shortfall or excess is settled on the employee's own return; the employer matches none of it.

questions.stem: An employer paid its state unemployment contributions on time all year. On 10 November its state still has federal advances outstanding. What is the effect on the employer's FUTA?
options: Its net FUTA rises for the whole calendar year, because the credit reduction is fixed by the position on 10 November
Only wages paid after 10 November bear the higher rate
Its state contributions rise, but its federal tax is unchanged
Nothing, because it paid its state contributions on time
questions.explanation: IRC § 3302(c)(2) reduces the credits otherwise allowable to employers in a state with outstanding advances, and because the reduction is determined by the position on 10 November it raises the net cost retrospectively for wages already paid in the year.

questions.stem: A courier's uninsured delivery van, adjusted basis $18,000 and worth $11,000 the day before, is totally destroyed in a flood. What is the casualty loss?
options: $11,000, the lesser of the decline in value and the adjusted basis
$18,000, because business property was totally destroyed and its value was below its basis
$7,000, the excess of basis over value
Nothing, because the van was worth less than its basis
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.165-7(b)(1), closing sentence, provides that where business property is totally destroyed and its fair market value immediately before the casualty is less than its adjusted basis, the adjusted basis is treated as the amount of the loss.

questions.stem: A fire destroys a business's warehouse and the insurance proceeds exceed its basis. The owner wants to reinvest in an apartment building thirty months later. Does IRC § 1033 defer the gain?
options: Yes, because like-kind real property qualifies and the period is three years
No, because IRC § 1033(g) requires a condemnation, so the general two-year period and the narrower replacement test apply
Yes, if the owner elects deferral on the return for the year of the fire
No, because a gain on destroyed property can never be deferred
questions.explanation: IRC § 1033(g) requires a seizure, requisition or condemnation of real property; a fire is not one, so the replacement must be similar or related in service or use under IRC § 1033(a)(2)(A) and made within the two-year period in IRC § 1033(a)(2)(B).

questions.stem: In 2026 a business discovers that an employee embezzled $90,000 in 2024. It sues the employee, who has assets, and settles the claim for $30,000 in 2027. In which year is the $60,000 loss deducted?
options: 2026, the year of discovery
2027, when the claim is resolved
2024, by amending that year's return
$90,000 in 2026, with $30,000 of income in 2027
questions.explanation: IRC § 165(e) puts a theft loss in the year of discovery, but IRC § 165(a) allows only a loss "not compensated for by insurance or otherwise," and a claim with a reasonable prospect of recovery postpones the deduction until the claim is resolved.

questions.stem: An unmarried management consultant has $250,000 of qualified business income and taxable income of $290,000 for 2026. What is her qualified business income deduction?
options: 20 percent of her qualified business income, with no wage test
A partial deduction, reduced ratably through the phase-in range
Nothing, because the practice is excluded entirely
The lesser of 20 percent of qualified business income and 50 percent of W-2 wages
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(d)(2) makes consulting a specified service trade or business, and under IRC § 199A(d)(3) a taxable income of $290,000 sits above the top of the 2026 phase-in range for an unmarried filer, so she has no qualified business income and no deduction.

questions.stem: A manufacturing business has $400,000 of qualified business income, pays $200,000 of W-2 wages, and holds qualified property with an unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition of $1,000,000. Its owner's taxable income is above the top of the phase-in range. What is the deduction for the business?
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(b)(2): the deduction is the lesser of 20 percent of qualified business income, $80,000, and the greater of 50 percent of wages, $100,000, or 25 percent of wages plus 2.5 percent of unadjusted basis, $75,000. The greater limitation is $100,000, which exceeds $80,000, so the limitation does not bite.

questions.stem: An unmarried taxpayer has $60,000 of qualified business income from a non-service business and $480,000 of investment income, giving taxable income of $540,000. Is she below the threshold amount for 2026?
options: Yes, because her business income is far below the threshold
No, because the threshold is measured on taxable income, which includes her investment income
Yes, because investment income is not qualified business income
No, because investment income is a specified service activity
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(e)(2) defines the threshold amount by reference to taxable income computed without the section's own deduction, so a taxpayer with modest business profits but large investment income can sit above it, and the wage and property limitation then applies in full.

questions.stem: A bakery had gross receipts of $1,400,000 last year and employed 22 full-time employees throughout it. It spends $9,000 making its entrance accessible and elects the section. Is it eligible for the disabled access credit?
options: No, because its gross receipts exceeded $1,000,000
Yes, because the employee-count alternative is satisfied and the two tests are alternatives
Yes, but the credit is reduced by half for exceeding the receipts test
No, because both the receipts test and the employee test must be met
questions.explanation: IRC § 44(b) confines the credit to a small business on either of two alternative tests, gross receipts for the preceding year or full-time employee count, and requires an election; a business passing the employee test need not pass the receipts test.

questions.stem: A corporation has net regular tax liability of $125,000, a tentative minimum tax of $40,000, no subpart A or B credits, and $95,000 of current year business credit. How much of the credit may it use this year?
questions.explanation: IRC § 38(c)(1) limits the credit to net income tax less the greater of the tentative minimum tax and 25 percent of net regular tax liability above $25,000; a quarter of $100,000 is $25,000, the tentative minimum tax of $40,000 is greater, and $125,000 less $40,000 leaves $85,000, with the remaining $10,000 going to IRC § 39.

questions.stem: A café takes the maximum disabled access credit on a $20,000 barrier-removal project. How is the portion of the expenditure that produced the credit treated?
options: It is also deducted in full under IRC § 190
It gets no further deduction or basis, while the rest of the spending is recovered under IRC § 190 or by depreciation
It is capitalised into the building and depreciated in addition to the credit
It is carried forward as an additional credit to the following year
questions.explanation: IRC § 44(d)(7) denies a double benefit for the amount that produced the credit; only the portion not taken into account for the credit is recovered under IRC § 190 to the extent that section applies, or otherwise capitalised and depreciated.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor has a $90,000 loss from her business and $5,000 of interest income. Her only other deduction is a $20,000 contribution to her own SEP retirement plan. What is her net operating loss?
questions.explanation: IRC § 172(d)(4)(D) excludes a IRC § 404 deduction made on behalf of a self-employed individual from the items treated as attributable to the trade or business, so the $20,000 is a non-business deduction allowed under IRC § 172(d)(4) only against her $5,000 of non-business income. The excess drops out and the loss is the $90,000 business loss alone.

questions.stem: A corporation carries a net operating loss that arose in a taxable year beginning in 2017 to its 2026 return. How is that loss treated?
options: Carried forward indefinitely, subject to the percentage cap
Carried forward twenty years, without the percentage cap, and absorbed before any post-2017 loss
Carried forward indefinitely without any cap
Carried back five years under the pandemic-era rule
questions.explanation: IRC § 172(a)(2)(A) takes losses from years beginning before 2018 first and without the cap; the carryover regime depends on the year the loss arose, and a pre-2018 loss keeps its twenty-year carryforward.

questions.stem: A corporation's only loss carryover is $1,000,000 arising in a taxable year beginning in 2023. Its 2026 taxable income before the net operating loss deduction is $500,000. How much may it deduct in 2026?
questions.explanation: IRC § 172(a)(2) caps the deduction for a loss arising after 2017 at 80 percent of taxable income computed without the IRC § 172, § 199A and § 250 deductions — 80 percent of $500,000. The remaining $600,000 carries forward indefinitely under IRC § 172(b)(1)(A)(ii).

questions.stem: A plumber works at customers' premises all day and spends evenings in a room used exclusively and regularly to prepare invoices and schedule jobs. He has no other fixed location for that work. Is the room his principal place of business?
options: No, because his income is earned at customers' premises
Yes, because administrative or management activities with no other fixed location for them make the home the principal place of business
Only if customers also meet him there
Only if the room is a separate structure
questions.explanation: IRC § 280A(c)(1), flush text, treats a home as the principal place of business where it is used for administrative or management activities and there is no other fixed location where the taxpayer conducts substantial administrative or management activities; the test is about where the administration happens, not where the money is earned.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor uses a 400 square foot room exclusively and regularly as her principal place of business and elects the safe harbour. What is her deduction?
questions.explanation: {fig:home.safe_harbor} (Rev. Proc. 2013-13 § 4.01) — a 400 square foot office exceeds the allowable square footage cap, so she gets the maximum the safe harbour permits, $1,500, and nothing for the excess footage.

questions.stem: A taxpayer filed her 2026 return using the safe harbour and now realises actual expenses would have given a larger deduction. What can she do?
options: Amend the 2026 return to switch to actual expenses
Nothing for 2026, but use actual expenses in 2027 without IRS consent
Nothing for 2026, and she must request IRS consent to change her method of accounting for 2027
Claim the difference as a carryover to 2027
questions.explanation: Rev. Proc. 2013-13 § 4.03 makes the choice irrevocable for the year once the return is filed, but it is made year by year and switching between the safe harbour and actual expenses is not a change in method of accounting, so no consent is needed for the next year.

questions.stem: A mother gives her son shares with a basis of $30,000 that are worth $90,000 on the date of the gift. He later sells them for $75,000. What does he report?
options: A $15,000 loss, measured against the value at the date of the gift
A $45,000 gain, because the donor's basis carries over for every purpose
Neither gain nor loss, because the price falls between the two figures
A $60,000 gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 1015(a): the dual basis arises only where fair market value at the date of the gift is below the donor's basis, so on appreciated property the $30,000 carryover basis governs gain and loss alike and the sale produces a $45,000 gain.

questions.stem: A company buys a machine: the invoice is $60,000 including sales tax, freight is $1,200, installation is $800, and it pays $3,000 for a one-year maintenance contract at the same time. What is the machine's basis?
questions.explanation: IRC § 1012(a) and IRC § 263(a)(1): the sales tax, freight and installation are costs of acquiring the machine and putting it into service, but the maintenance contract is a service to be received over the following year, not a cost of the asset.

questions.stem: A beneficiary inherits stock and sells it at a gain 40 days after the decedent's death. The gain is:
options: Short-term, because she held the stock for only 40 days
Long-term, because property whose basis is determined under IRC § 1014 is treated as held for more than one year
Long-term only if the decedent had held it for more than one year
Ordinary income, because inherited property is not a capital asset
questions.explanation: IRC § 1223(9): where basis is determined under IRC § 1014 and the property is sold within one year of the death, the holder is considered to have held it for more than one year, so the acquisition route rather than the actual holding period decides the character.

questions.stem: Machinery that cost $100,000 and has $60,000 of accumulated depreciation is sold for $115,000. How is the gain characterised?
options: $75,000 of ordinary income
$60,000 of ordinary income under IRC § 1245 and $15,000 of IRC § 1231 gain
$75,000 of IRC § 1231 gain
$15,000 of ordinary income and $60,000 of IRC § 1231 gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 1245(a)(1): the lower of recomputed basis ($100,000) and the amount realised ($115,000), less the $40,000 adjusted basis, is ordinary income — $60,000 — and only the remaining $15,000 of gain enters the IRC § 1231 netting.

questions.stem: In 2026 a business has a net IRC § 1231 gain of $150,000. It deducted net IRC § 1231 losses of $100,000 in 2020 and $40,000 in 2022, neither yet recaptured. What is the character of the 2026 gain?
options: $140,000 ordinary and $10,000 long-term capital gain
$40,000 ordinary and $110,000 long-term capital gain
$150,000 long-term capital gain
$100,000 ordinary and $50,000 long-term capital gain
questions.explanation: IRC § 1231(c): the pool is the non-recaptured net losses of the five most recent preceding taxable years, so the 2022 loss is recaptured as ordinary while the 2020 loss has dropped out of the rolling window.

questions.stem: A business sells a building for $300,000 cash, and the buyer assumes the $450,000 mortgage on it. The adjusted basis is $500,000. What is the gain or loss?
options: No gain until the mortgage is paid off
questions.explanation: IRC § 1001(b): the amount realised includes debt the buyer assumes or takes subject to, so it is $750,000, and IRC § 1001(a) measures the gain against the $500,000 adjusted basis.

questions.stem: Kessler Holdings, a calendar-year C corporation, transfers relinquished real property on 20 December 2026 and does not extend its 2026 return. By when must it receive the replacement property?
options: 180 days after the transfer, in June 2027
The due date of its 2026 return, because that date comes before the 180th day
45 days after the transfer
The end of 2027
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(a)(3)(B): the exchange period ends at the earlier of 180 days after the transfer or the due date of the return for the year of the transfer, so with no extension taken a late-year relinquishment runs out of time in March, well before the 180th day in June.

questions.stem: A company exchanges a building with an adjusted basis of $400,000, subject to a $100,000 mortgage the other party assumes, for real property worth $650,000 with no cash changing hands. What is recognised, and what is the new basis?
options: No gain, and a basis of $400,000
$100,000 of gain, and a basis of $400,000
$100,000 of gain, and a basis of $500,000
$350,000 of gain, and a basis of $650,000
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(d) treats a liability assumed, determined under IRC § 357(d), as money received, so IRC § 1031(b) recognises gain to the $100,000 of boot; the basis is $400,000 less the $100,000 treated as received plus the $100,000 recognised.

questions.stem: A developer exchanges one of its subdivision lots, held for sale to customers, for a parcel it will hold for investment. Does IRC § 1031 apply?
options: Yes, because real property was exchanged for real property
No, because real property held primarily for sale is excluded
Yes, provided the parcel is identified within 45 days
No, because a developer can never hold real property for investment
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(a)(2): the section is unavailable for real property held primarily for sale, so a dealer's inventory and a developer's lots are outside it however like-kind the replacement is.

questions.stem: A taxpayer converts a residence with an adjusted basis of $200,000 to a rental when it is worth $150,000, takes $30,000 of depreciation, and sells it for $195,000. What does she report?
options: A $25,000 gain
A $75,000 gain, measured against the loss basis
Nothing, because the price is below her original cost
A $5,000 loss
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.165-9(b)(2) caps only the basis for determining loss; no provision caps the gain basis, which is the original $200,000 less $30,000 of depreciation, or $170,000, so a sale at $195,000 produces a $25,000 gain.

questions.stem: A business expensed a truck in full under IRC § 179, converted it to the owner's personal use two years ago, and now sells it for $12,000. What is reported on the sale?
options: Nothing, because the truck was personal-use property when sold
$12,000 of ordinary income, because recapture applies to a later disposition of converted property
$12,000 of long-term capital gain
Nothing, because the recapture was recognised at the conversion
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.168(i)-4(c) recognises no gain, loss or recapture on the conversion itself but provides that IRC § 1245 and § 1250 apply to any later disposition of the converted property, so IRC § 1245(a)(1) makes the whole $12,000 ordinary against a nil basis.

questions.stem: A car cost $40,000 and was converted to business use when worth $30,000. After $8,000 of depreciation it is destroyed with no insurance recovery. What is the maximum basis for the casualty loss?
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.165-7(a)(5): the casualty basis on converted property is the lesser of adjusted basis and fair market value at conversion, adjusted for depreciation since — $30,000 less $8,000 — so the value the car lost before the conversion never enters the deduction.

questions.stem: Ashby Retail owns a $3,000,000 store and spends $35,000 replacing the building's entire electrical system. Its preparer argues the cost is trivial next to the building. Is it capitalised?
options: No, because $35,000 is immaterial relative to the building's cost
Yes, because the test runs against the electrical system as its own unit, and replacing the whole system is a restoration
No, because electrical work is always a deductible repair
Yes, but only if the work extended the building's useful life
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.263(a)-3(e)(2)(ii) makes each building system a separate unit from the structure, and replacing the whole of a system is the replacement of a major component — a restoration under Reg. § 1.263(a)-3(k)(1)(vi); comparing the cost to the building answers a question the regulation does not ask.

questions.stem: Loring Fabrication has no applicable financial statement, had accounting procedures in place from 1 January, expenses small items on its books, and attaches the de minimis statement to its timely return. It buys twelve tools at $2,100 each on one invoice listing each separately, and a $3,800 compressor on another. Which may it expense under the safe harbor?
options: All of them, because the invoices together fall under the annual cap
The twelve tools, because each is within the without-AFS ceiling, but not the compressor
None, because the tools' invoice total exceeds the ceiling
All of them, because a taxpayer without an AFS uses the higher ceiling
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.263(a)-1(f)(1)(ii): without an applicable financial statement the ceiling applies per invoice or per item as substantiated by the invoice, so each $2,100 tool qualifies while the $3,800 compressor exceeds it, and there is no annual cap in either direction.

questions.stem: While capitalising a roof replacement, Pemberton pays $4,000 to repair ceiling plaster damaged by the roofing work and, on the same day, $2,500 to repaint an unrelated office. How are the two amounts treated?
options: Both deductible as repairs under Reg. § 1.162-4
Both capitalised, because they were incurred at the same time as an improvement
The $4,000 is capitalised as an indirect cost incurred by reason of the improvement, and the $2,500 is deductible
The $2,500 is capitalised and the $4,000 is deductible
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.263(a)-3(g)(1)(i) capitalises indirect costs incurred by reason of an improvement even where they would have been deductible alone, while work merely performed at the same time that benefits nothing about the improvement stays deductible.

questions.stem: A domestic LLC with three members files no Form 8832 and no Form 2553. For federal tax purposes it is:
options: A corporation, because an LLC gives its members limited liability
A partnership by default, filing Form 1065
A disregarded entity reported on each member's own return
An association, because it has more than one member
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.7701-3(b)(1)(i): a domestic eligible entity with two or more members is a partnership unless it elects otherwise, so it files under IRC § 6031(a) and furnishes each member a Schedule K-1; limited liability drives only the foreign defaults.
questions.pageTitle: Proper business type, and the use of classification codes and year to year comparison

questions.stem: Delacroix Studio LLC files Form 8832 on 10 September specifying an effective date of 1 May of the same year, more than 75 days before the filing date. The election:
options: Is invalid, and the entity keeps its default classification
Takes effect on 1 May as specified
Takes effect 75 days before the filing date
Takes effect on the filing date, 10 September
questions.explanation: Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iii): a specified date more than 75 days before filing does not invalidate the election; it takes effect 75 days before the filing date, so the entity files two returns for the year, one for each classification.
questions.pageTitle: Proper business type, and the use of classification codes and year to year comparison

questions.stem: Whitlow Goods buys raw materials, supplies them to a subcontractor who produces the finished product, and retains title throughout. Which principal business activity code does it use?
options: A wholesale trade code, because it operates no factory
A manufacturing code, because it retains title to the goods being produced
A professional services code, because it manages the subcontractor
The subcontractor's own code
questions.explanation: Instructions for Form 1120-S, Principal Business Activity Codes: a company that buys raw materials, supplies them to a subcontractor to produce the finished product, and retains title is a manufacturer and must use a manufacturing code.
questions.pageTitle: Proper business type, and the use of classification codes and year to year comparison

questions.stem: Brightwater Retail's books expense the full cost of client meals, while the return deducts only the portion the Code allows. Into which category of book-to-tax difference does this fall?
options: Timing
Classification
Error
Permanent
questions.explanation: A permanent difference is an item that counts for one purpose and never for the other, and the disallowed portion of the meals never becomes deductible; it belongs on the reconciliation that Reg. § 1.446-1(a)(4) names as a required accounting record, not in an amended return.

questions.stem: A wholesaler reports cost of goods sold of $800,000 and tells the examiner it marks up everything 25 percent over cost. What gross receipts does that statement imply?
options: $1,066,667, treating 25 percent as the margin
$1,000,000, a margin of 20 percent on the selling price
questions.explanation: IRM 4.10.3.11.1 computes the gross profit ratio on the selling price, so a 25 percent markup on $800,000 of cost gives sales of $1,000,000 and a $200,000 gross profit that is 20 percent of receipts; reading 25 percent as a margin would imply receipts near $1,066,667 and a spurious adjustment.

questions.stem: A company's income statement shows $14,000 of interest and $30,000 of rent below an "operating income" subtotal. The preparer leaves both off the return as not arising from the business. Is that correct?
options: Yes, because non-operating income is reported by the shareholders
Yes, provided the amounts fall below a reporting threshold
No, because IRC § 61(a) takes income from whatever source derived and the subtotal is only a presentation
No for the rent, but the interest may be omitted
questions.explanation: IRC § 61(a) defines gross income as all income from whatever source derived and lists interest and rents by name, so the split between operating and non-operating revenue is a presentational distinction the return ignores.

questions.stem: A bookkeeper lists accounts payable of $40,000, accrued wages of $12,000, inventory of $75,000 and a note payable of $150,000 as the liabilities of the business. Which item does not belong in that total?
options: Accrued wages, because they are not yet due
Inventory, because it is an asset
The note payable, because long-term debt is equity
Accounts payable, because they are offset by receivables
questions.explanation: IRM 4.10.3.10.1 defines assets as the resources owned and liabilities as the debts owed, and the identity is assets equal liabilities plus equity; inventory is a resource owned, so it sits on the asset side and the liabilities total $202,000.
questions.pageTitle: Balance sheet (e.g., proofing beginning and ending balances, relationship to income statement and depreciation)

questions.stem: Renshaw Products Inc. has total receipts of $90,000 for the year and total assets of $600,000 at year end. Must it complete Schedule L on Form 1120?
options: No, because total receipts are under the exception threshold
No, provided the Schedule K question is answered affirmatively
Yes, because the exception requires both total receipts and total assets to be under the threshold
Yes, and it must file Schedule M-3 in place of Schedule M-1
questions.explanation: The Instructions for Form 1120, Schedule L, set a two-part test on two different figures, total receipts and total assets at year end, each under the threshold; failing either limb means Schedules L, M-1 and M-2 are all required.
questions.pageTitle: Balance sheet (e.g., proofing beginning and ending balances, relationship to income statement and depreciation)

questions.stem: An examiner reviewing a balance sheet under IRM 4.10.3.10.3 must choose accounts for in-depth analysis. Which account is most likely to be selected?
options: The largest account on the balance sheet, because size drives risk
A small account with an unusual title and many adjusting journal entries
The cash account, because it is always examined first
Any account whose balance changed during the year
questions.explanation: IRM 4.10.3.10.3 selects accounts for their behaviour, not their size: unusual titles, unusual entries, many adjusting journal entries, or a concentration of large entries in one month, so a large but ordinary account may never be examined.
questions.pageTitle: Balance sheet (e.g., proofing beginning and ending balances, relationship to income statement and depreciation)

questions.stem: Ferris Tooling, a calendar-year C corporation, has used an impermissible method of accounting for five years and wants to report correctly from 2026. What must it do?
options: Simply begin using the correct method in 2026, because moving to a permissible method requires no consent
File amended returns for the open years and use the correct method going forward
Obtain the Commissioner's consent, generally by filing Form 3115, even though the old method was impermissible
Continue the old method until the IRS raises the issue on examination
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.446-1(e)(2)(i): consent is required whether or not the method being changed from was proper, so self-correction is itself an unauthorised change and forfeits the audit protection a Form 3115 change would carry.
questions.pageTitle: Method of accounting and changes (e.g., accrual, cash, hybrid, Form 3115)

questions.stem: Bellamy Corp, a calendar-year C corporation, had gross receipts of $29,000,000, $34,000,000 and $36,000,000 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and expects $25,000,000 in 2026. May it use the cash method for 2026?
options: Yes, because the three-year average including 2026 is within the threshold
No, because the average of 2023 through 2025 exceeds the 2026 threshold
Yes, because its 2026 receipts alone are within the threshold
No, because a C corporation may never use the cash method
questions.explanation: IRC § 448(c)(1) and Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 3.30: the average runs over the three taxable years ending with the year preceding the year tested, and $33,000,000 is above the 2026 figure, so the § 448(a) prohibition applies; a preparer who averaged 2024 through 2026 would reach the wrong answer.
questions.pageTitle: Method of accounting and changes (e.g., accrual, cash, hybrid, Form 3115)

questions.stem: Pruett Catering, a cash-method taxpayer, pays $9,000 on 1 October 2026 for a service contract running 24 months from that date. How much may it deduct in 2026?
options: $9,000, because a cash-method taxpayer deducts what it pays
Nothing in 2026, because a cash-method taxpayer may never deduct a prepayment
Only the portion allocable to 2026, because the benefit runs beyond the 12-month window and the prepayment is capitalised
$9,000, because the 12-month rule covers any prepayment of two years or less
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.263(a)-4(f)(1): the 12-month rule relieves capitalisation only where the benefit does not extend beyond the earlier of 12 months after it is first realised or the end of the following taxable year, and a 24-month contract fails both limbs, so it is capitalised and recovered over the period it covers whatever method the taxpayer uses.
questions.pageTitle: Method of accounting and changes (e.g., accrual, cash, hybrid, Form 3115)

questions.stem: A machine that cost $80,000 has accumulated depreciation of $50,000 and is sold for $25,000. How much ordinary income does IRC § 1245 produce?
options: $50,000, the depreciation taken
$25,000, the amount realised
$5,000, the difference between basis and proceeds
None, because the sale produces a $5,000 loss
questions.explanation: IRC § 1245(a)(1) takes the lower of the depreciation figure and the excess of amount realised over adjusted basis, and with basis of $30,000 against $25,000 realised there is no excess; recapture reclassifies gain and never creates it, so the result is a $5,000 § 1231 loss.

questions.stem: A passenger automobile is placed in service in year one at 70 percent qualified business use and depreciated under MACRS. In year three qualified business use falls to 45 percent. What happens in year three?
options: Depreciation for year three is reduced proportionately and nothing else changes
The car moves to the alternative depreciation system for year three onward, and the excess depreciation for years one and two is included in income
Nothing until the car is sold, when the full depreciation is recaptured
The car moves to the alternative depreciation system prospectively, with no income inclusion
