questions.explanation: IRC § 280F(b)(1) requires the alternative depreciation system for that year and all later years, and IRC § 280F(b)(2)(A) includes the excess depreciation in gross income in the year of the drop, measured against what the alternative system would have allowed from the start.

questions.stem: Larch Cabinetry expensed a $50,000 saw under IRC § 179 in a year when a loss carryforward meant the election saved no tax. Two years later the saw ceases to be used predominantly in the business. Is there recapture?
options: No, because the election produced no tax benefit
No, because recapture requires a sale or exchange
Yes, measured against what IRC § 168 would have allowed through the year of recapture, regardless of whether the deduction reduced tax
Yes, but only under the IRC § 280F(b) predominant-use rule
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.179-1(e)(1) triggers on the property ceasing to be used predominantly in a trade or business, compares the amount expensed with what IRC § 168 would have allowed through the year of recapture, and applies whether or not the excess reduced tax liability; the saw is not listed property, so § 280F is not involved.

questions.stem: Calloway Partners makes a $20,000 cash contribution to a public charity. On the partnership's own return, the contribution is:
options: Deducted in computing ordinary business income, because the partnership made the gift
A separately stated item passed through to the partners, who apply their own percentage limitations
Disallowed entirely, because a partnership cannot make a deductible gift
Deducted by the partnership only if every partner itemizes
questions.explanation: IRC § 703(a)(2)(C) denies the partnership the IRC § 170 deduction, and IRC § 702(a)(4) makes the contribution a separately stated item tested against each partner's own contribution base, because only the partner knows which limitation applies.
questions.pageTitle: Pass-through activity (e.g., K-1, separately stated items, non-deductible expenses)

questions.stem: A partner begins the year with basis of $60,000. Her Schedule K-1 shows $25,000 of ordinary income, a $40,000 cash distribution, and a $70,000 share of a separately stated loss. How much of the loss may she deduct this year?
options: $70,000 in full
$45,000, with $25,000 carried forward
$60,000, with $10,000 carried forward
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(d) allows the loss only to the extent of basis, and the adjustments run in order: increase for income to $85,000, decrease for the distribution to $45,000, then the loss is allowed to that extent and the remaining $25,000 carries forward indefinitely until basis is restored.
questions.pageTitle: Pass-through activity (e.g., K-1, separately stated items, non-deductible expenses)

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder with stock basis of $20,000 lends the corporation $50,000 directly. Her share of the year's loss is $60,000. How much is deductible?
options: $20,000, because only stock basis counts against a loss
$60,000, because stock basis plus basis in the direct loan exceeds the loss
$50,000, because the loan alone limits the loss
$60,000, because losses of an S corporation are never limited
questions.explanation: IRC § 1366(d)(1) allows losses up to the sum of stock basis and the adjusted basis of indebtedness of the corporation to the shareholder — $70,000 here — so the full $60,000 passes through; the second tier exists because the debt runs from the corporation to her directly, which a guarantee would not provide.
questions.pageTitle: Pass-through activity (e.g., K-1, separately stated items, non-deductible expenses)

questions.stem: Corwin Industries, a C corporation, has gross receipts of $60,000,000 and total assets of $7,500,000 on the last day of its tax year. Which reconciliation schedule does it file?
options: Schedule M-3, because its receipts exceed the partnership receipts test
Schedule M-1, because the corporate trigger is total assets and they are below the threshold
Schedule M-3 Part I, with Schedule M-1 in place of Parts II and III
Neither, because a corporation of that size files only Schedule M-2
questions.explanation: Instructions for Form 1120, Schedule L: the Form 1120 trigger is total assets on the last day of the tax year, a balance sheet figure, and receipts decide nothing for a corporation; only the Form 1065 rule adds a receipts test.
questions.pageTitle: Reconciliation of tax versus books (e.g., M-1, M-2, M-3)

questions.stem: A C corporation reports total assets of $30,000,000 on the last day of its tax year. What may it file?
options: Schedule M-1 alone, because it is under the upper band
Schedule M-3 in full, with no relief available
Schedule M-3 Part I, with Schedule M-1 in place of Parts II and III
Schedule M-2 in place of both reconciliation schedules
questions.explanation: IRM 4.10.3.8: a corporation or partnership with at least $10 million but under $50 million of total assets at year end may file Schedule M-1 in place of Schedule M-3 Parts II and III, while Part I remains required of everyone at $10 million or more.
questions.pageTitle: Reconciliation of tax versus books (e.g., M-1, M-2, M-3)

questions.stem: For a partnership, Schedule M-1 reconciles net income per the books to:
options: Taxable income before the net operating loss deduction and special deductions
Ordinary business income before any separately stated item
Net income per Schedule K, after every separately stated income and expense item
Partners' ending capital on Schedule M-2
questions.explanation: IRM 4.10.3.8.1: for an S corporation or a partnership the schedule ends at income per Schedule K after all separately stated items, whereas the C corporation version ends at taxable income before the net operating loss and special deductions, because a pass-through has no taxable income.
questions.pageTitle: Reconciliation of tax versus books (e.g., M-1, M-2, M-3)

questions.stem: Ostrander sells land with a basis of $500,000 to her wholly owned corporation for its $420,000 appraised value. The corporation later sells the land to an unrelated buyer for $470,000. What does the corporation recognise?
options: $50,000 of gain
No gain, because the $50,000 is sheltered by Ostrander's disallowed loss
A $30,000 loss, measured against Ostrander's original basis
$50,000 of gain, with Ostrander now allowed her $80,000 loss
questions.explanation: IRC § 267(d)(1): the transferee's gain is recognised only to the extent it exceeds the loss disallowed to the transferor under § 267(a)(1), so $50,000 is fully sheltered by the $80,000 disallowed loss, and the unused $30,000 is never deducted by anyone.

questions.stem: Maddox owns a 60 percent profits interest in a partnership and sells it a building at a $35,000 loss for its appraised value. The loss is:
options: Allowed, because IRC § 267 reaches only individuals and corporations
Disallowed under IRC § 707(b)(1), because he owns more than 50 percent of the profits interest
Allowed, because the sale was at appraised value
Deferred until his profits interest falls to 50 percent or less
questions.explanation: IRC § 707(b)(1) disallows losses on sales between a partnership and a person owning more than 50 percent of its capital or profits interest, and like § 267 it has no arm's length exception, so the appraisal is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Two related persons exchange like-kind real property. Twenty months after the last transfer one of them dies, and the executor sells the property received. Is the exchange unwound?
options: Yes, because a disposition by either party within two years unwinds it
No, because dispositions after the death of either the taxpayer or the related person are excepted
Yes, unless the estate reacquires like-kind property
No, because only a disposition by the original taxpayer counts
questions.explanation: IRC § 1031(f)(2): a disposition after the death of the taxpayer or of the related person is one of the three exceptions to the two-year rule in § 1031(f)(1), alongside compulsory conversions and dispositions with no tax-avoidance purpose.

questions.stem: Bramley Interiors, an S corporation, pays its sole shareholder $5,000 a month recorded as "loan to shareholder". There is no note, no stated interest, no maturity, and no repayment in three years. How will an examiner treat the balance?
options: As a below-market loan, with interest imputed under IRC § 7872
As a distribution under IRC § 1368, tax-free to the extent of the accumulated adjustments account and stock basis and then gain
As a genuine loan, with no consequence until it is forgiven
As a loan, once the shareholder signs a note covering the earlier advances
questions.explanation: Without a note, an adequate rate, a maturity and actual payments the advance is not debt, so IRC § 1368 governs rather than IRC § 7872, which presupposes a loan; adding a note now does not make the earlier advances a loan.

questions.stem: Coldharbour Ltd, a C corporation, lends its sole shareholder $300,000 interest-free on a genuine written demand note that the shareholder services on request. What are the consequences at the end of the calendar year?
options: None, because no interest was paid in cash
The shareholder alone has a deemed distribution; the corporation has nothing to report
The whole $300,000 is recharacterised as a distribution
Forgone interest is treated as transferred from the corporation to the shareholder and retransferred as interest, giving the corporation interest income and the shareholder a deemed distribution
questions.explanation: IRC § 7872(a) creates a deemed transfer and a deemed retransfer on the last day of the calendar year for a corporation-shareholder loan within § 7872(c)(1)(C), so both parties have tax consequences although no cash moves.

questions.stem: An S corporation shareholder's note was reduced to a basis of $20,000 against a $60,000 face by earlier losses. During the year the corporation repays the note in full and also has a $50,000 net increase in pass-through items. Where does the net increase go first?
options: To stock basis, because stock is always restored before debt
To the repaid note, to the extent needed to offset the gain that would otherwise arise on the repayment
Pro rata across stock basis and all outstanding debts
Nowhere, because a repaid note can no longer carry basis
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.1367-2(c) applies a net increase first to restore basis in indebtedness repaid during the year to the extent needed to offset gain on the repayment, then to the remaining outstanding debts, and only then to stock basis.

questions.stem: Aldwick Partners LLP had six partners on 1 January; one left in March and a new partner joined in November, so six were partners at year end. It files its Form 1065 two months after the due date with no reasonable cause. How many monthly penalty units apply under IRC § 6698?
options: Twelve, six partners for two months
Fourteen, seven partners for two months
Seven, one unit per partner
Two, one unit per month
questions.explanation: IRC § 6698(b) multiplies the monthly figure by the number of persons who were partners during any part of the year, not the partners at year end, so seven partners for two months gives fourteen units.
questions.pageTitle: Reporting and filing obligations (e.g., extended returns and potential penalties, international information returns, Form 1099 series, Form 8300)

questions.stem: Bewley Contracting discovers in early February that it failed to file forty Forms 1099-NEC that were due on 31 January. Which filing date keeps each form at the lowest tier of the IRC § 6721 penalty?
options: Filing by 1 August
Filing within 30 days of the required filing date
Filing by the extended due date of Bewley's own return
Filing at any time before the Service issues a notice
questions.explanation: IRC § 6721: the penalty falls to the lowest tier if the return is filed within 30 days of the required filing date, to the middle tier if filed by 1 August, and the general rule applies thereafter.
questions.pageTitle: Reporting and filing obligations (e.g., extended returns and potential penalties, international information returns, Form 1099 series, Form 8300)

questions.stem: A business fails both to file thirty Forms 1099-NEC with the Service and to furnish the corresponding statements to the thirty payees. How many penalties does each form carry?
options: One, because the statement is a copy of the return
One, with the amount doubled for the missing statement
Two, one under IRC § 6721 and one under IRC § 6722, each with its own amount and cap
None until the Service issues a notice and demand
questions.explanation: IRC § 6721 penalises the return not filed with the Service and IRC § 6722 penalises the statement not furnished to the payee; they are separate provisions with separate amounts and separate caps, so every form carries two penalties.
questions.pageTitle: Reporting and filing obligations (e.g., extended returns and potential penalties, international information returns, Form 1099 series, Form 8300)

questions.stem: Tarrant Joinery reported $38,000 of employment taxes in its lookback period. Its payroll doubles during the current year, so the year's employment taxes will reach about $90,000, but no single day's accumulation ever approaches the next-day threshold. What is its deposit schedule this year?
options: Monthly for the whole year, because status is fixed by the lookback period
Semi-weekly from the month in which cumulative taxes pass the annual line
Semi-weekly for the whole year, because this year's taxes exceed the line
Next-day, because the payroll has doubled
questions.explanation: Reg. § 31.6302-1(b): depositor status is an annual determination made on the aggregate employment taxes reported for the lookback period, and growth during the year does not change it — only the next-day rule in Reg. § 31.6302-1(c)(3) alters status mid-year.
questions.pageTitle: Payments and deposit obligations (e.g., employment tax, excise tax)

questions.stem: Ovington Design, in its second quarter of having employees, accumulates $1,400 of withheld income tax and FICA for the quarter, and its first quarter was smaller still. What must it do with the $1,400?
options: Deposit it by electronic funds transfer by the 15th of the following month
It may remit the amount with a timely filed return for the quarter, and the deposit is deemed timely made
Deposit it within three business days after the end of the quarter
Deposit it by the close of the next day after the last payroll
questions.explanation: Reg. § 31.6302-1(f)(4): an employer whose accumulated employment taxes for a return period fall below the de minimis threshold may remit them with a timely filed return, and the same relief carries forward where the immediately preceding quarter was also below it.
questions.pageTitle: Payments and deposit obligations (e.g., employment tax, excise tax)

questions.stem: Wardle Freight fails to deposit $40,000 of employment taxes, receives a delinquency notice from the Service, and makes the deposit twelve days after the notice. What penalty rate applies under IRC § 6656?
options: 10 percent
5 percent
15 percent
2 percent
questions.explanation: IRC § 6656(b)(1)(B): the rate rises to 15 percent where the tax is not deposited within 10 days after the first delinquency notice, so the elapsed-days tiers of § 6656(b)(1)(A) are displaced once the notice has issued and ten days have passed.
questions.pageTitle: Payments and deposit obligations (e.g., employment tax, excise tax)

questions.stem: Kestle Surveys operates a plan that meets all three accountable plan requirements. An employee receives a $4,000 advance, substantiates $3,100 of expenses within the deadline, and keeps the remaining $900 without returning it. How much is treated as wages?
options: The whole $4,000, because the excess was not returned
$900 only
Nothing, because the arrangement itself qualifies
$3,100, the amount substantiated
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.62-2(c)(2)(ii): where the arrangement meets the requirements but the employee fails to return an excess within a reasonable period, only the amounts not exceeding the substantiated expenses are treated as paid under an accountable plan, so the $900 alone becomes wages.
questions.pageTitle: Record-keeping requirements (e.g., mileage log, accountable plans)

questions.stem: Instead of fixed deadlines, an employer gives each employee a statement every quarter showing amounts paid in excess of substantiated expenses, and requires substantiation or return within 120 days of the statement. Is the return-of-excess requirement within a safe harbour?
options: No; the only safe harbour is return within 120 days after the expense is paid or incurred
No; the statements would have to be issued monthly
Yes; the periodic statement method deems action within 120 days of a quarterly statement timely
No; the safe harbours apply only to advances, not to returns of excess
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.62-2(g)(2)(ii): where the payor gives employees a statement no less often than quarterly showing amounts in excess of substantiated expenses and asks for substantiation or return within 120 days of the statement, action within that period is timely.
questions.pageTitle: Record-keeping requirements (e.g., mileage log, accountable plans)

questions.stem: A consultant kept no contemporaneous record of her business travel and offers credit card statements alone to establish the business purpose of each trip. Is that sufficient under the fallback route?
options: Yes, because the statements establish the amount and the date of each charge
Yes, provided the charges are to airlines and hotels
No, because the fallback route is unavailable for travel expenses
No; the fallback needs her own detailed statement and corroborative evidence, and a card statement proves only amount and date
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.274-5T(c)(3)(i) is conjunctive — a detailed statement and other corroborative evidence — and a credit card statement establishes an amount and a date while saying nothing about business purpose, the element most often in dispute.
questions.pageTitle: Record-keeping requirements (e.g., mileage log, accountable plans)

questions.stem: Lyndhurst Castings, a C corporation with substantial earnings and profits, pays its sole shareholder-officer $600,000 in a year when comparable executives earn $200,000 to $260,000. The officer genuinely runs the business full time. How is the excess treated?
options: It is deductible in full, because the services were actually rendered
It is not deductible, but there is no consequence to the shareholder
It is not deductible and is a constructive dividend to the shareholder to the extent of earnings and profits
It is recharacterised as wages and subjected to employment tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 162(a)(1) allows only a reasonable allowance for compensation for services actually rendered, and the disallowed portion becomes a constructive dividend taxed under IRC § 301(c) — the double taxation the payment was designed to avoid.

questions.stem: An owner materially participates in her operating company and rents it a warehouse she owns. A roof replacement this year turns the rental into an $18,000 loss. How is the loss characterised?
options: Non-passive, because the property is rented to a business in which she materially participates
Passive, because the self-rental rule recharacterises income only
Non-passive, and deductible against her salary from the company
Disallowed entirely, because the parties are related
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.469-2(f)(6) treats gross rental income from property rented for use in a trade or business in which the taxpayer materially participates as non-passive up to the net rental income from the property; a loss year stays passive, which is the asymmetry that gives the taxpayer the worst of both regimes.

questions.stem: A partner performs services for the partnership, and the partnership then makes an allocation of income and a distribution to that partner that are linked to those services. How are the steps analysed?
options: Under the disguised payment rule, as a transaction between the partnership and a non-partner where the steps viewed together are properly so characterised
Under the disguised sale rule, as a sale of property to the partnership
As an ordinary distributive share and distribution, because that is what the documents call them
As a contribution to capital followed by a nonrecognition distribution
questions.explanation: IRC § 707(a)(2)(A): a performance of services by a partner, coupled with a related allocation and distribution to that partner, is recharacterised where the two viewed together are properly a transaction between the partnership and a non-partner — the disguised sale rule in IRC § 707(a)(2)(B) is the counterpart for a transfer of property followed by a transfer back.

questions.stem: Pellow Systems, an S corporation, issues non-voting common stock to a key employee. The non-voting shares carry exactly the same rights to distributions and liquidation proceeds as the voting shares. What happens to the S election?
options: It terminates, because the corporation now has two classes of stock
It continues, because differences in voting rights alone are permitted
It continues only if the employee is a family member of an existing shareholder
It terminates unless the non-voting shares are converted within the year
questions.explanation: IRC § 1361(b)(1)(D) denies eligibility to a corporation with more than one class of stock, but the test is about rights to distribution and liquidation proceeds; differences in voting power alone do not create a second class.
questions.pageTitle: Selection of business entity (e.g., benefits and detriments)

questions.stem: Wexcombe Inc., an S corporation, has 99 shareholders, all unrelated resident individuals, and one class of stock. On 12 May it issues stock to two more unrelated individuals. What is the result?
options: The election continues, because 101 shareholders is within the ceiling
The election terminates on 31 December of that year
The election terminates on 12 May, when the corporation first has more than 100 shareholders
The election continues if the new shareholders sign consents
questions.explanation: IRC § 1361(b)(1)(A) denies eligibility to a corporation with more than 100 shareholders, and the stock issue that takes the count past the line terminates the election from that date rather than at year end.
questions.pageTitle: Selection of business entity (e.g., benefits and detriments)

questions.stem: Two owners hold a business 50/50. They want 70 percent of the depreciation deductions allocated to the owner who contributed most of the capital. Which entity form permits that?
options: An S corporation, by shareholder agreement
Either form, provided the allocation is disclosed on the return
A partnership, if the allocation has substantial economic effect under IRC § 704(b)
Neither form, because allocations must always follow ownership
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(b) lets a partnership allocate items other than in proportion to capital where the allocation has substantial economic effect; an S corporation must allocate strictly per share per day.
questions.pageTitle: Selection of business entity (e.g., benefits and detriments)

questions.stem: Pellow Consulting, a C corporation with substantial earnings and profits, pays for its sole shareholder's $30,000 family holiday and deducts it as travel. What are the consequences?
options: The deduction is denied and nothing further follows
The deduction is denied and the $30,000 is a constructive dividend taxed to the shareholder
The deduction is allowed because the payment was ordinary and necessary to keep the shareholder working
The deduction is denied and the $30,000 reduces the shareholder's stock basis
questions.explanation: IRC § 262(a) denies the deduction for a personal, living or family expense whatever account paid it, and the payment is then a constructive distribution taxable under IRC § 301(c) to the extent of earnings and profits — the second consequence a careless answer leaves out.
questions.pageTitle: Comingling (e.g., personal usage of business accounts, separation of business and personal accounts)

questions.stem: An activity consisting in major part of breeding and showing horses reported net income in years 2 and 5 of the seven consecutive years ending with the current year, and losses in the other five. Does the IRC § 183(d) presumption apply for the current year?
options: Yes; the horse variant requires only 2 profitable years of 7
No; the presumption requires 3 profitable years of 5
No; the presumption requires 3 profitable years of 7
Yes, and the Secretary may no longer establish the contrary
questions.explanation: IRC § 183(d) requires gross income to exceed the attributable deductions in 2 or more of 7 consecutive years for an activity consisting in major part of breeding, training, showing or racing horses — but it only shifts the burden, and the Secretary may still establish that the activity is not engaged in for profit.
questions.pageTitle: Comingling (e.g., personal usage of business accounts, separation of business and personal accounts)

questions.stem: On examination, five of the nine factors in Reg. § 1.183-2(b) point toward a profit motive and four point against it. What follows?
options: The activity is engaged in for profit, because a majority of the factors favour the taxpayer
The activity is engaged in for profit only if at least six factors favour the taxpayer
The activity is not engaged in for profit, because the businesslike-manner factor is decisive
Nothing on its own; the determination is not made by counting factors on each side
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.183-2(b) says in terms that no single factor is determinative, that the list is not exhaustive, and that the determination is not made by comparing how many factors fall each way.
questions.pageTitle: Comingling (e.g., personal usage of business accounts, separation of business and personal accounts)

questions.stem: Kelsall Print has for five years deducted the owner's personal club dues as a business expense. A new preparer wants to correct the treatment. What is the correct instrument?
options: Amended returns for the open years, because a non-timing item is not a method however consistently treated
Form 3115, because five years of consistency has made the treatment a method
Form 3115 under the automatic procedures, with a section 481(a) adjustment for the cumulative dues
Nothing, because consistent treatment has fixed the character of the item
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.446-1(e)(2)(ii)(b) excludes from the definition of a change in method an item that does not involve the proper time for inclusion or deduction, giving the example of items deducted as business expenses that are in fact personal; the dues are barred by IRC § 262(a) and never a timing question.
questions.pageTitle: Advice on accounting methods and procedures (e.g., explanation of requirements)

questions.stem: Pennock Supply, a C corporation, meets the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test for 2026 on its average annual gross receipts for the three taxable years ending with the preceding year. Which provisions does passing the test lift?
options: The cash method bar only
The cash method bar and the inventory requirement, but uniform capitalisation still applies
The cash method bar, the inventory requirement and the uniform capitalisation rules, all at once
The uniform capitalisation rules only
questions.explanation: IRC § 448(c) relieves the IRC § 448(a) cash method bar, and the same test lifts IRC § 471(a) and IRC § 263A — a single computation opens three doors, which is why it is the efficient first step.
questions.pageTitle: Advice on accounting methods and procedures (e.g., explanation of requirements)

questions.stem: Dunmore Freight keeps its books under generally accepted accounting principles, but shifts the treatment of certain gross income items from one year to the next while staying within those principles each year. Does the safe harbour in Reg. § 1.446-1(a)(2) apply?
options: Yes; conformity to generally accepted accounting principles is sufficient on its own
No; the safe harbour requires that all items of gross income and expense be treated consistently from year to year
Yes, provided a Form 3115 is filed for each year in which the treatment shifts
No; a method based on generally accepted accounting principles never clearly reflects income
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.446-1(a)(2) treats consistent application of generally accepted accounting principles as ordinarily clearly reflecting income only provided all items of gross income and expense are treated consistently from year to year — book conformity without consistency is not the safe harbour.
questions.pageTitle: Advice on accounting methods and procedures (e.g., explanation of requirements)

questions.stem: A partner holding a 10 percent interest contributes land worth $250,000 with a basis of $90,000 to the partnership in exchange for an increased interest, after which she holds 15 percent. What does she recognise?
options: $160,000 of gain, because she does not control the partnership afterwards
Nothing, because IRC § 721(a) has no control requirement
$160,000 of gain, because a later contribution by an existing owner is a sale
Nothing, but only if the land is held for seven years
questions.explanation: IRC § 721(a) asks only that property be contributed for a partnership interest, with no control requirement and no solely-for-stock equivalent, so a later contribution by an existing minority owner is non-recognition; the same facts would fail the control test of IRC § 351.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer of property in or out of the business (e.g., contributed property, distributions)

questions.stem: Partner A contributes $300,000 in cash; partner B contributes land with a basis of $100,000 and a value of $300,000. They share profits equally. Two years later the partnership sells the land for $340,000. How much of the gain is allocated to B?
questions.explanation: IRC § 704(c)(1)(A) allocates the $200,000 of gain built in at contribution to the contributor, and only the $40,000 of post-contribution appreciation is shared, so B takes $200,000 plus $20,000.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer of property in or out of the business (e.g., contributed property, distributions)

questions.stem: Farrant Holdings, a C corporation, distributes land with a basis of $200,000 and a fair market value of $650,000 to its sole shareholder. What does the corporation recognise?
options: Nothing, because a distribution to a shareholder is not a sale
$450,000 of gain, and the shareholder is also taxed on the distribution
$450,000 of gain, with the shareholder receiving the land tax-free
Nothing now, with the gain deferred until the shareholder sells the land
questions.explanation: IRC § 311(b)(1) recognises gain to the corporation as if the appreciated property had been sold at fair market value, and IRC § 301(c) then taxes the shareholder on the distribution, so two levels of tax fall on one movement of property.
questions.pageTitle: Transfer of property in or out of the business (e.g., contributed property, distributions)

questions.stem: Brackley Holdings, a C corporation, distributes a building worth $1,500,000 with an adjusted basis of $400,000 to its sole shareholder in complete liquidation. The shareholder's stock basis is $300,000. What is recognised?
options: $1,200,000 of gain by the shareholder only
$1,100,000 of gain by the corporation only
No gain at either level, because a liquidation is a nonrecognition event
$1,100,000 of gain by the corporation and $1,200,000 of gain by the shareholder
questions.explanation: IRC § 336(a) recognises gain to the corporation as if the building had been sold to the shareholder at fair market value, and IRC § 331(a) treats the shareholder as receiving full payment in exchange for the stock, so both layers apply and neither is elective.
questions.pageTitle: Life cycle of the business (e.g., formation, dissolution)

questions.stem: A calendar-year S corporation files a revocation on 1 March with the consent of shareholders holding 60 percent of its shares, and specifies no prospective date. When does the revocation take effect?
options: 1 January of the current year
1 January of the following year
1 March of the current year
It is invalid, because every shareholder must consent
questions.explanation: IRC § 1362(d)(1): a revocation needs the consent of shareholders holding more than one half of the shares, and one made on or before the 15th day of the third month takes effect from the first day of that year unless a prospective date is specified.
questions.pageTitle: Life cycle of the business (e.g., formation, dissolution)

questions.stem: A partner with an outside basis of $120,000 retires and receives $150,000 in cash from the partnership, which continues its business with the remaining partners. What does the partner recognise?
options: $150,000 of gain, the full amount received
$30,000 of gain, to the extent the money exceeds outside basis
Nothing, because a partnership distribution is never a recognition event
$30,000 of gain, recognised by the partnership rather than the partner
questions.explanation: IRC § 731(a): a departing partner has gain only to the extent money distributed exceeds outside basis, in contrast to a corporate liquidation, where IRC § 336(a) and IRC § 331(a) tax both the entity and the owner.
questions.pageTitle: Life cycle of the business (e.g., formation, dissolution)

questions.stem: A sole proprietor manages investment portfolios for clients, pays no W-2 wages, and has taxable income above the top of the section 199A phase-in range. For section 199A the business is:
options: Not a specified service trade or business, because the section 1202 list does not name investment management
A qualified trade or business subject only to the wage and property limitation
A specified service trade or business, so the deduction is excluded entirely
A specified service trade or business entitled to a reduced deduction under the applicable percentage
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(d)(2)(B) adds investing and investment management to the specified service list beyond what section 1202 names, and above the top of the phase-in range a specified service business gets nothing.
questions.pageTitle: Type of industry (e.g., specified service business owners)

questions.stem: A sole proprietor running a small law practice has $80,000 of qualified business income and taxable income well below the section 199A threshold. What deduction does she take?
options: None, because law is a specified service trade or business
A reduced deduction under the applicable percentage in IRC § 199A(d)(3)
The full 20 percent deduction, because specified service status is disregarded below the threshold
A deduction limited by the W-2 wages the practice pays
questions.explanation: IRC § 199A(b)(3) disregards specified service status for a taxpayer below the threshold, and the wage and property limitations are disregarded there as well, so she takes the full 20 percent on her qualified business income.
questions.pageTitle: Type of industry (e.g., specified service business owners)

questions.stem: Holloway Farms, a farming business, has average annual gross receipts far above the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test. May it use the cash method?
options: No, because a business above the gross receipts test must use an accrual method
Yes, because IRC § 448(b)(1) lifts the cash method prohibition for a farming business regardless of receipts
Only if it is a qualified personal service corporation
Only for contracts it expects to complete within two years
questions.explanation: IRC § 448(b)(1) removes the cash method bar for a farming business without regard to gross receipts; the gross receipts test is what other businesses rely on, and the two-year rule belongs to the IRC § 460(e) construction exception.
questions.pageTitle: Type of industry (e.g., specified service business owners)

questions.stem: Maybury Life engages a full-time life insurance salesman who meets both statutory employee conditions. Which reporting combination is correct?
options: Form 1099-NEC, with the earnings and expenses on Schedule C and self-employment tax on Schedule SE
Form W-2 with the statutory employee box checked, social security and Medicare withheld, no income tax withholding, and earnings and expenses on Schedule C
Form W-2 reported as wages, with income tax and FICA withheld and no expense deduction
Form W-2 with the statutory employee box checked, and self-employment tax paid on Schedule SE
questions.explanation: IRC § 3121(d)(3)(B) makes the full-time life insurance salesman a statutory employee: FICA is withheld by the payer, income tax is not, and the income and related expenses go on Schedule C, so no self-employment tax is due.
questions.pageTitle: Worker classification (i.e. independent contractor versus employee, outside sales, full-time vs part-time)

questions.stem: Thorne Realty's licensed agents are paid entirely on commission and have no minimum hours, but there is no written agreement with any of them. What is their status under IRC § 3508?
options: Qualified real estate agents, because two of the three requirements are met
Qualified real estate agents, provided a contract is signed before the year-end filings
IRC § 3508 does not apply, and classification falls back to the common law test
Statutory employees under IRC § 3121(d)(3)
questions.explanation: IRC § 3508(b)(1)(C) requires the services to be performed under a written contract providing that the individual will not be treated as an employee for federal tax purposes; without it the section does not apply, and a contract signed later does nothing for years already filed.
questions.pageTitle: Worker classification (i.e. independent contractor versus employee, outside sales, full-time vs part-time)

questions.stem: Culver Freight treated a driver as a contractor, filed no Form 1099-NEC or Form W-2, and cannot show reasonable cause. On examination the driver is an employee with $100,000 of wages. Under IRC § 3509, the income tax withholding component of Culver's liability is:
options: $1,500, at the reduced 1.5 percent rate
$3,000, at the doubled 3 percent rate
The full amount that should have been withheld from the driver
Nothing, because the employer's own FICA share is all that remains payable
questions.explanation: IRC § 3509(b)(1) doubles the § 3509(a) rates to 3 percent and 40 percent where the employer also failed the information reporting requirements without reasonable cause; the employer's own FICA share and FUTA stay payable in full on top.
questions.pageTitle: Worker classification (i.e. independent contractor versus employee, outside sales, full-time vs part-time)

questions.stem: Hartwell Stores spends $250,000 replacing the roof on the store building it has operated for years, and has ample taxable income from the business. Which cost recovery route reaches the roof?
options: Bonus depreciation, automatically, because the roof is qualified property
Either route, at the taxpayer's choice
An IRC § 179 election, because a roof on non-residential real property is qualified real property
Neither; only ordinary depreciation is available for a structural component
questions.explanation: IRC § 179(e) treats qualified real property, including a roof on non-residential real property placed in service after the building was, as eligible for the election, while a structural component of non-residential real property is outside IRC § 168(k).
questions.pageTitle: Deductions and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses, NOL, depreciation versus IRC Section 179 versus bonus depreciation)

questions.stem: Glenmore Tooling qualifies for $150,000 of general business credits and expects tax liability of $170,000. Its preparer proposes expensing $500,000 of new equipment, which would cut the liability to $20,000. What happens to the credit the year cannot absorb?
options: It is carried forward indefinitely with no carryback
It is refunded to the extent it exceeds the liability
It is lost once the year's liability is exhausted
It is carried back one year and forward twenty
questions.explanation: IRC § 38 limits the general business credit by tax liability, with unused amounts carried back one year and forward twenty — so a deduction that reduces liability to nothing strands the credit for a long deferral rather than saving tax.
questions.pageTitle: Deductions and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses, NOL, depreciation versus IRC Section 179 versus bonus depreciation)

questions.stem: A cash-method business prepays three years of insurance premiums in December to bring the whole deduction into the current year. What is the result?
options: The prepayment is capitalised, because it reaches beyond the 12-month window regardless of the taxpayer's method
The whole premium is deductible, because a cash-method taxpayer deducts when it pays
The whole premium is deductible under the recurring item exception
The whole premium is deductible only if the business is on an accrual method
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.263(a)-4(f) capitalises a prepayment reaching beyond the 12-month window whatever the method, so year-end prepayment does not accelerate the deduction; what works is paying amounts already incurred or completing services before year end.
questions.pageTitle: Deductions and credits for tax planning (e.g., timing of income and expenses, NOL, depreciation versus IRC Section 179 versus bonus depreciation)

questions.stem: Whitcombe Foods averaged 41 full-time employees and full-time equivalents on business days during 2025. It expands early in 2026 and averages 70 for that year. Is it an applicable large employer for 2026?
options: Yes, from the first month of 2026 in which its workforce exceeds 50
Yes, for the whole of 2026, because the 2026 average exceeds 50
No, because only a two-year average is counted
No; its 2026 status was fixed by the 2025 average, although it will be one for 2027
questions.explanation: IRC § 4980H(c)(2)(A): an applicable large employer is one that employed an average of at least 50 full-time employees on business days during the preceding calendar year, so nothing done during 2026 changes its 2026 status.

questions.stem: Two corporations under common control employ 40 and 35 full-time employees respectively. Neither offers coverage, and one employee of the smaller company obtains a premium tax credit. On how many employees is the no-coverage payment computed?
options: 15; each company takes its own reduction of 30
45; the combined 75 less a single reduction of 30 allocated between the two companies
75; no reduction is available to an aggregated group
1; only the employee who received the credit
questions.explanation: IRC § 4980H(c)(2)(C)(i) treats persons treated as a single employer under IRC § 414(b), (c), (m) or (o) as one employer, and IRC § 4980H(c)(2)(D)(ii) allows one reduction of 30 for the group, allocated among its members, not one each.

questions.stem: An applicable large employer offers every full-time employee coverage that is affordable and provides minimum value, and no employee obtains a premium tax credit. It files no Forms 1094-C or 1095-C for the year. What is its exposure?
options: Per-return and per-statement penalties under IRC §§ 6721 and 6722, even though no assessable payment is due
Nothing, because no assessable payment arose
The no-coverage payment on its whole full-time workforce less 30
The offered-coverage payment on the employees it failed to report
questions.explanation: IRC §§ 6055 and 6056 require the returns regardless of whether any assessable payment arises, and a failure is an information return failure penalised under IRC §§ 6721 and 6722 — reporting and liability are separate obligations.

questions.stem: A trust's instrument requires all income to be distributed annually and has no charitable provision. In 2026 the trustee also distributes $80,000 of corpus; in 2027 it distributes income only. How is the trust classified?
options: Complex for 2026 and every later year
Complex for 2026 and simple again for 2027
Simple in both years, because corpus is not income
A grantor trust for 2026
questions.explanation: IRC § 651(a): simple describes a year, not an instrument. The trust must both satisfy the terms test and not in fact distribute amounts other than income for the year, so distributing corpus fails the second limb for 2026 only.
questions.pageTitle: Trust types (e.g., simple/complex, grantor, irrevocable, tax shelters, foreign)

questions.stem: A settlor creates an irrevocable trust for her children with no power to revoke, no reversion and no right to income, but retains in a non-fiduciary capacity a power to reacquire trust assets by substituting property of equivalent value. Who reports the trust's income?
options: The trust, because it is irrevocable
The settlor, as owner under the administrative-powers rule in IRC § 675
The settlor, but only if a reversion exceeds 5 percent
The children, as beneficiaries
questions.explanation: IRC § 675(4)(C) treats a power of administration exercisable in a non-fiduciary capacity, including a power to reacquire the corpus by substituting property of equivalent value, as making the grantor the owner, and IRC § 671 attributes the items to her. Irrevocability is irrelevant to that provision.
questions.pageTitle: Trust types (e.g., simple/complex, grantor, irrevocable, tax shelters, foreign)

questions.stem: A trust settled by a United States citizen has trustees who are all United States persons and who control every substantial decision, but it is administered in Bermuda and only a Bermuda court can supervise its administration. Domestic or foreign?
options: Domestic, because United States persons control all substantial decisions
Foreign, because the court test fails and both tests must be met
Domestic, because the settlor is a United States person
Foreign only if a beneficiary is a non-resident alien
questions.explanation: IRC § 7701(a)(30)(E) requires both that a court within the United States be able to exercise primary supervision over the administration and that United States persons control all substantial decisions. A trust administered abroad fails the court test, and IRC § 641(b) then treats it as a non-resident alien individual.
questions.pageTitle: Trust types (e.g., simple/complex, grantor, irrevocable, tax shelters, foreign)

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the IRC § 643(a) modifications made to taxable income in computing distributable net income?
options: The distribution deduction is added back
The exemption is added back
Capital gains allocated to corpus are excluded
Depreciation is added back
questions.explanation: IRC § 643(a): the modifications are no distribution deduction, no exemption, capital gains allocated to corpus excluded, extraordinary dividends excluded for simple trusts, tax-exempt interest added net of allocable expenses, and the IRC § 1202 exclusion disregarded. Depreciation stays deducted, which is why a rental trust's distributable net income falls below its accounting income.
questions.pageTitle: Distributable net income and accounting income

questions.stem: A simple trust is required to distribute $50,000 of income to its beneficiary for the year. Its distributable net income is $38,000. What may the trust deduct, and what does the beneficiary include?
questions.explanation: IRC § 651(b): where the income required to be distributed exceeds distributable net income the deduction is limited to distributable net income, and IRC § 652(a) limits the beneficiary's inclusion to the same figure. Distributing more than distributable net income never enlarges either side.
questions.pageTitle: Distributable net income and accounting income

questions.stem: A simple trust receives a one-off special dividend that the trustee, acting in good faith, allocates to corpus under the instrument and local law. For fiduciary accounting income purposes the dividend is:
options: Income, because dividends are always income
Not income, so the trustee is not required to distribute it currently
Income to the extent of distributable net income
Income, but taxed to the trust
questions.explanation: IRC § 643(b): items of gross income constituting extraordinary dividends or taxable stock dividends that the fiduciary in good faith determines to be allocable to corpus under the instrument and local law are not income for this purpose, and the IRC § 643(a) modifications exclude them from a simple trust's distributable net income as well.
questions.pageTitle: Distributable net income and accounting income

questions.stem: Which of the following can never claim the IRC § 642(c) charitable deduction?
options: An estate
A complex trust whose instrument directs charitable payments
A simple trust
A trust created after 1969
questions.explanation: IRC § 642(c)(1) excludes a trust meeting the specifications of subpart B, a simple trust, which is consistent because a trust whose instrument permits charitable payments can never be simple in the first place. A post-1969 trust loses only the set-aside limb, not the deduction for amounts paid.

questions.stem: Of the four IRC § 642(b) exemptions, which one is adjusted for inflation each year?
options: The estate's exemption
The ordinary trust's exemption
The exemption for a trust required to distribute all income currently
The qualified disability trust exemption
questions.explanation: IRC § 642(b)(2)(C); Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 3.35: the qualified disability trust figure is tied to the personal exemption amount and restated annually, while the estate, ordinary trust and current-distribution trust figures have stood unchanged since 1954.

questions.stem: A trust created in 2019 permanently sets aside $25,000 of gross income for a charity under its instrument but pays nothing to the charity during the year or the following year. Is a deduction available?
options: Yes, under IRC § 642(c), because a set-aside is treated the same as a payment
Yes, under IRC § 170(a)
No, the set-aside limb does not reach most trusts created after 1969, though an estate could use it
Yes, but limited to a percentage of the trust's income
questions.explanation: IRC § 642(c): a deduction for amounts permanently set aside rather than paid is available to an estate and to certain older trusts but not to most trusts created after 1969, and IRC § 170(a) is no fallback because the fiduciary deduction applies in lieu of it.

questions.stem: An examination establishes that $40,000 of a taxpayer's underpayment is attributable to fraud arising from an abusive trust arrangement. What is the IRC § 6663 penalty?
questions.explanation: IRC § 6663 imposes a penalty of 75 percent of the portion of an underpayment attributable to fraud, so $30,000. The promoter's exposure under IRC § 6700 and a preparer's under IRC § 6701 are separate from it.

questions.stem: A preparer knowingly prepares four Forms 1041 implementing an abusive trust arrangement after the client explains candidly that the purpose is to reduce tax. How does IRC § 6701 apply?
options: Not at all, because the client directed the treatment
As a single penalty for the engagement
As a penalty per document, so on each of the four returns
Only if the preparer also sold the arrangement
questions.explanation: IRC § 6701(a) imposes a penalty per document on a person who aids or assists in preparing any portion of a return knowing it would understate another person's liability; the client's candour establishes the knowledge element rather than excusing the preparer.

questions.stem: A promoter tells a client that transferring assets to a trust the client will continue to control removes them from the client's estate as a completed gift. Is that correct?
options: Yes, because any transfer to a trust is a completed gift
No, because a gift is complete only where the donor has irrevocably parted with dominion and control, so contributing to a grantor trust generally produces no completed gift
Yes, provided the trust is labelled irrevocable
No, because gifts to trusts are never complete
questions.explanation: IRS abusive trust guidance: a gift is complete to the extent the donor has irrevocably parted with dominion and control, so a structure designed to leave the grantor in control generally produces no completed gift, and that is the same fact that defeats the income tax claim.

questions.stem: Neither a trust's instrument nor applicable local law says how sale proceeds are to be treated. The trustee sells an investment. The proceeds are allocated to:
options: Income, because they are receipts of the year
Principal
Distributable net income automatically
Income and principal in equal shares
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.643(b)-1: under the default allocation dividends, interest and rents are generally allocated to income, while proceeds from the sale or exchange of trust assets generally go to principal.

questions.stem: A trust's income is defined by state statute as a 4 percent unitrust amount, which comes to $40,000 for the year. Distributable net income computed without capital gains is $28,000. The trustee has discretion to allocate gains to income. What is the most gain the trustee may allocate to income?
options: Nothing, because gains are always principal
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.643(a)-3(b)(1): where income is a unitrust amount and the fiduciary has discretion to allocate gains to income, the amount so allocated is capped at the excess of the unitrust amount over distributable net income computed without it, here $40,000 less $28,000.

questions.stem: Under its instrument a trust pays $50,000 of capital gain to a charity and takes an IRC § 642(c) deduction for it. May the trustee keep the gain out of distributable net income as an amount allocated to corpus?
options: Yes, because gains allocated to corpus are always outside distributable net income
Yes, at the fiduciary's election
No, because gains for which a charitable deduction is allowed must be included in distributable net income
No, because charitable payments are never deductible by a trust
questions.explanation: Reg. § 1.643(a)-3(c): capital gains paid, permanently set aside or to be used for IRC § 642(c) purposes, so that a charitable deduction is allowed for them, must be included in distributable net income. It is not a fiduciary election; it prevents a deduction for an amount that never entered the computation.

questions.stem: A trust has distributable net income of $100,000 and no charitable deduction. Its instrument requires $60,000 of income to be paid to A. The trustee also distributes $50,000 each to B and C under a discretionary power. What does B report?
options: Nothing, because the first tier absorbs distributable net income
questions.explanation: IRC § 662(a)(2): where the two tiers together exceed distributable net income, each second-tier beneficiary includes a proportionate share of what remains after the first tier, so the $40,000 left after A's $60,000 is shared between B and C in the ratio of their other amounts, $20,000 each.
questions.pageTitle: Separately stated items (items reported on the K-1)

questions.stem: A complex trust's instrument requires $70,000 of income to be paid to A and $35,000 to B. Distributable net income is $72,000 after an $18,000 charitable deduction. What does A report?
questions.explanation: IRC § 662(a)(1): where the income required to be distributed to all beneficiaries exceeds distributable net income, each first-tier beneficiary includes a proportionate share of distributable net income computed without the charitable deduction, $90,000, so A takes 70/105 of $90,000. Using the $72,000 figure is the common error.
questions.pageTitle: Separately stated items (items reported on the K-1)

questions.stem: Before a trust's classes of income are apportioned among beneficiaries, how are the deductions entering into distributable net income, including the IRC § 642(c) charitable deduction, treated?
options: Deducted entirely from taxable interest
Allocated among the classes of income under the regulations, with a required allocation of indirect expenses to tax-exempt income first
Ignored, because beneficiaries report gross amounts
Allocated wholly to whichever class the trustee selects
questions.explanation: IRC § 662(b): distributable net income is a net figure, and the deductions inside it are allocated among the classes of income under the regulations before the classes are shared out, indirect expenses proportionately, with a required allocation to tax-exempt income first and some fiduciary discretion over the rest.
questions.pageTitle: Separately stated items (items reported on the K-1)

questions.stem: An estate has gross income of $475 for its taxable year and, after expenses, taxable income of $150. Must it file Form 1041?
options: Yes, because it has taxable income
No, because an estate files only where gross income is $600 or more
Yes, because every estate files for each year of administration
No, because an estate never files until administration closes
questions.explanation: IRC § 6012(a)(3) applies only the $600 gross income threshold to an estate; the "any taxable income" limb in IRC § 6012(a)(4) is a trust rule, and a trust in the same position would have to file.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, tax years, and penalties

questions.stem: A calendar-year complex trust obtains an extension for its 2026 Form 1041. What is the extended due date?
options: 15 October 2027
30 September 2027
15 September 2027
15 August 2027
questions.explanation: IRC § 6072(a) puts the return on the fifteenth day of the fourth month after the year closes, 15 April, and the IRC § 6081 extension for a fiduciary return is five and a half months rather than six, which lands on 30 September rather than 15 October.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, tax years, and penalties

questions.stem: A complex trust files its Form 1041 four months late. It distributed all of its distributable net income and owes no tax. What penalty exposure does it face?
options: A per-beneficiary monthly penalty of the kind IRC § 6698 imposes on partnerships
The IRC § 6651 additions, which are a percentage of the tax due and so produce nothing here
Loss of the distribution deduction for the year
A penalty measured by distributable net income
questions.explanation: IRC § 6651 imposes the failure to file and failure to pay additions in the ordinary way, as a percentage of the tax due, and there is no per-beneficiary penalty of the kind IRC §§ 6698 and 6699 impose on partnerships and S corporations, so a trust that distributed everything may owe nothing.
questions.pageTitle: Filing requirements, tax years, and penalties

questions.stem: A charity's articles are impeccable. In practice, 40 percent of its budget goes to running a commercial catering business unrelated to any exempt purpose, with every dollar of profit funding its literacy programme. Does it qualify under IRC § 501(c)(3)?
options: Yes, because the organisational test is met and the profits go to charity
No, because a single substantial non-exempt purpose defeats the operational test regardless of the exempt purposes beside it
Yes, provided the catering income is reported on Form 990-T
No, because any commercial activity at all is prohibited
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.501(c)(3)-1(c): the operational test is an activity test, and a substantial non-exempt purpose defeats exemption no matter how many exempt purposes accompany it; passing the organisational test does not carry over, and the destination of the income is not the test.
questions.pageTitle: Qualifying for and maintaining tax-exempt status (e.g., IRC 501(c))

questions.stem: A disqualified person receives a $60,000 excess benefit from a charity and does not correct it within the taxable period. What taxes fall on the disqualified person?
options: $15,000 initial tax and $120,000 additional tax
$6,000 initial tax and $120,000 additional tax
$15,000, and the charity loses its exemption
questions.explanation: IRC § 4958(a) imposes an initial tax of 25 percent of the excess benefit on the disqualified person, and IRC § 4958(b) adds 200 percent where it is not corrected within the taxable period; the 10 percent tax falls on the managers, and the charity's exemption is not automatically lost.
questions.pageTitle: Qualifying for and maintaining tax-exempt status (e.g., IRC 501(c))

questions.stem: A church that lobbies modestly wants certainty and asks to make the IRC § 501(h) expenditure election. Which is correct?
options: It may elect, like any IRC § 501(c)(3) organisation
It may not elect, because churches and their integrated auxiliaries are excluded, so the substantial part test governs
It may elect only after filing the IRC § 508 notice
It need not elect, because churches may lobby without limit
questions.explanation: IRC § 501(h): the election is closed to churches and their integrated auxiliaries, which also stand outside the IRC § 508 notice requirement, so a church's lobbying is measured under the substantial part test with no numerical safe harbour.
questions.pageTitle: Qualifying for and maintaining tax-exempt status (e.g., IRC 501(c))

questions.stem: A charity incorporated on 10 January 2024 submits Form 1023 on 15 March 2026 and receives a favourable determination letter in September 2026. From what date is its exemption effective?
options: 10 January 2024
15 March 2026
The date of the determination letter in September 2026
31 January 2024
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.508-1(a)(2)(i) gives 15 months from the end of the month of formation and Treas. Reg. § 301.9100-2(a)(2)(iv) adds an automatic 12 months, so the window ran from 31 January 2024 to 30 April 2026; the application was inside it, and recognition runs from the date of formation.
questions.pageTitle: Applying for IRS tax-exempt status (e.g., Form 1023, Form 1024)

questions.stem: A new nonprofit corporation, not a church, school, hospital, LLC or successor to a for-profit, projects gross receipts of $38,000, $44,000 and $58,000 in its first three years and holds $30,000 of assets. May it file Form 1023-EZ?
options: Yes, because its average projected receipts over the three years are within the limit
Yes, because its assets are far below the asset limit
No, because projected receipts in any one of the next three years above the limit make it ineligible
No, because a corporation must always file the full Form 1023
questions.explanation: Form 1023-EZ Eligibility Worksheet, questions 1 through 3: an organisation projecting annual gross receipts over the limit in any of the next three years may not use the short form, and the test is year by year, not an average; a single "yes" on the worksheet sends the file to Form 1023.
questions.pageTitle: Applying for IRS tax-exempt status (e.g., Form 1023, Form 1024)

questions.stem: A charity submits Form 1023 on 1 February 2026, answers every Service request promptly, and by 1 December 2026 has received no determination. What is its position?
options: It may withdraw and refile to restart the clock without losing anything
It is deemed to have exhausted its administrative remedies and may seek a declaratory judgment under IRC § 7428
No court has jurisdiction until a final adverse determination letter issues
It must file a 30-day protest to preserve any right to go to court
questions.explanation: IRC § 7428(b)(2): an organisation that took all reasonable steps in a timely manner is deemed to have exhausted its remedies 270 days after the request, and that date has passed; withdrawing the application would forfeit the route, because withdrawal is neither a failure to determine nor exhaustion.
questions.pageTitle: Applying for IRS tax-exempt status (e.g., Form 1023, Form 1024)

questions.stem: A calendar-year charity in its fifth year had gross receipts of $31,000, $36,000 and $74,000 in 2024, 2025 and 2026, and holds $20,000 of assets. What is the least it may file for 2026?
options: Form 990-EZ only, because 2026 receipts alone exceed the Form 990-N ceiling
Form 990-N, because gross receipts are normally within the ceiling on the three-year average
Form 990, because an organisation more than three years old must file the full return
Form 990-PF
questions.explanation: IRC § 6033(i): the electronic notice is available where gross receipts are normally within the ceiling, and for an organisation at least three years old that is measured as an average over the three years including the year being tested — here $47,000 — not against the single year.

questions.stem: An organisation with gross receipts of $2,400,000 files its 2026 Form 990 in 2027, 40 days late, with no reasonable cause. Applying the amounts for returns required to be filed in 2027, what is the penalty?
questions.explanation: IRC § 6652(c)(1)(A): an organisation whose gross receipts exceed the indexed large-organisation line pays the higher daily rate, $130 for 2027 filings, so 40 days is $5,200, well under the $66,500 cap; $25 a day is the ordinary tier and $20 the unindexed statutory figure.

questions.stem: A calendar-year charity files Form 8868 on 10 May 2027 for its 2026 Form 990, then in October asks for three more months. What is the position?
options: A second Form 8868 gives a further three months
The extension is a single automatic six months to 15 November 2027, and no further extension exists
The extension runs only to 15 October, the individual filing date
The Form 8868 was invalid because it was not filed by 15 April
questions.explanation: IRC § 6072(e) sets the due date at the 15th day of the 5th month, 15 May for a calendar year; Form 8868 gives one automatic six-month extension to 15 November, and there is no second extension.

questions.stem: A charity runs a food stand for the two weeks of the county fair each year, staffed by paid workers, and the $18,000 it nets goes entirely into its programmes. Is the income unrelated business taxable income?
options: Yes, because the stand is a trade or business and selling food is not related
No, because the profits are used for the exempt purpose
No, because a stand run for two weeks a year is not regularly carried on
Yes, because paid staff defeat the volunteer labour exception
questions.explanation: Treas. Reg. § 1.513-1(c): frequency and continuity measured against comparable commercial activity decide the second test, and a two-week stand at a fair is the regulation's own example of a business not regularly carried on; the use of the profits is expressly irrelevant under IRC § 513(a).

questions.stem: A charity owns an office building outright and leases one floor to a firm. Which lease term would cause the rent to lose the IRC § 512(b)(3) exclusion?
options: Rent set at 6 percent of the tenant's gross receipts
Rent set at 20 percent of the tenant's net profits
A lease that includes office furniture accounting for a tenth of the total rent
A ten-year term with fixed annual increases
questions.explanation: IRC § 512(b)(3): the exclusion fails where the rent depends on the income or profits of any person from the property other than by a fixed percentage of receipts or sales, or where more than half the rent is attributable to personal property; a percentage-of-gross-receipts lease and incidental furniture rent are both fine.

questions.stem: A sponsor pays a charity $25,000 for its gala. The agreement displays the sponsor's name and logo and provides that $5,000 of the payment is refundable if attendance falls below 400. How is the payment treated?
options: Entirely a qualified sponsorship payment
Entirely advertising income, because any contingency taints the whole payment
$20,000 is a qualified sponsorship payment and the $5,000 contingent on attendance is not
Entirely excluded as a charitable contribution
questions.explanation: IRC § 513(i)(2)(B)(i) takes any payment contingent on attendance outside the definition, and IRC § 513(i)(3) splits the payment so that the portion which would qualify on its own remains a qualified sponsorship payment.

questions.stem: An employee aged 45 works for two corporations that are members of the same controlled group. She defers $10,000 into each corporation's 401(k) and each corporation contributes $30,000 to her account. Is any limit breached for 2026?
options: No, because each plan's annual additions of $40,000 are inside the limit on their own
Yes, the annual additions limit, because the two employers are aggregated and $80,000 exceeds $72,000
Yes, the elective deferral limit, because $20,000 of deferrals must be aggregated across employers
No, because annual additions are only ever tested plan by plan
questions.explanation: IRC § 415(c) applies per employer, but employers aggregated under IRC § 414(b), (c), (m) or (o) count as one, so a controlled group has a single annual additions limit for the participant; her $20,000 of deferrals is inside the IRC § 402(g) limit.

questions.stem: In February 2027 a participant discovers a $2,000 excess deferral for 2026 and allocates it to one plan. She has extended her 2026 return to 15 October 2027. By when must the plan distribute the excess to avoid double taxation?
options: 15 April 2027, and the extension does not move it
15 October 2027, the extended due date of her return
1 March 2027, the allocation date
31 December 2027, the end of the following plan year
questions.explanation: Under IRC § 402(g) the participant allocates the excess by 1 March and the plan distributes it, with allocable income, by 15 April; that is a hard statutory date rather than the filing deadline in disguise, and a missed distribution leaves the excess taxed twice.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old joins a new employer on 1 January 2026, having earned $200,000 of wages from her previous employer in 2025. She wants to make a pre-tax catch-up contribution to the new employer's 401(k). Must the catch-up be a designated Roth contribution?
options: Yes, because her 2025 wages exceeded the threshold
No, because the threshold looks only at prior-year wages from the employer sponsoring the plan, and she had none
Yes, unless the new plan has no Roth feature
No, because catch-up contributions are never required to be Roth
questions.explanation: IRC § 414(v)(7) measures the preceding calendar year's IRC § 3121(a) wages from the sponsoring employer, so a participant's first year with a new employer is never caught by it.

questions.stem: An S corporation is owned equally by two unrelated 2 percent shareholders. Its retirement plan covers the two shareholders and their spouses and no one else. Which annual return does the plan file?
options: Form 5500
Form 5500-SF, because four participants is fewer than 100
Form 5500-EZ
None, because the plan has no common-law employees
questions.explanation: IRC § 1372(b): a 2 percent shareholder of an S corporation is treated as a partner, so a plan covering only partners and their spouses is a one-participant plan and files Form 5500-EZ; Form 5500-SF may no longer be used in its place.

questions.stem: A plan administrator files Form 8955-SSA 30 days late, omitting four participants who separated with deferred vested benefits. Leaving reasonable cause aside, what is the penalty?
options: $10 a day regardless of participants, so $300
$10 per omitted participant per day, so $1,200
$50 per omitted participant, so $200
questions.explanation: IRC § 6652(d): failure to file a complete IRC § 6057(a) registration statement costs $10 for each participant omitted multiplied by the number of days the failure continues, capped at $50,000 for the plan year; the $250 daily rate belongs to the Form 5500 penalty under IRC § 6652(e).

questions.stem: A sponsor discovers that its one-participant plan never filed the Form 5500-EZ returns due for three plan years. Which route to penalty relief is open to it?
options: The Department of Labor's Delinquent Filer Voluntary Compliance Program
The Service's penalty relief programme under Rev. Proc. 2015-32, or reasonable cause
Filing Form 5558 retroactively for each year
Filing the late returns on Form 5500-SF through EFAST2 instead
questions.explanation: Rev. Proc. 2015-32: the Service's own programme, or ordinary reasonable cause, is the route for a delinquent Form 5500-EZ. The Department of Labor programme is the answer for a delinquent Form 5500 or Form 5500-SF and is unavailable for a one-participant plan.

questions.stem: An employer with a SEP wants to exclude a 19-year-old who has worked for it in each of the last four years and earned $30,000 last year. May it?
options: No, because service in three of the preceding five years is enough on its own
Yes, because the employee has not attained age 21
No, because part-time and young employees can never be excluded from a SEP
Yes, because employees under 25 may always be excluded
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(k)(2) requires an employee to be covered only once they have attained age 21, performed service in at least three of the immediately preceding five years, and received at least the threshold compensation; the age test is not met.
questions.pageTitle: Plans for self-employed persons (e.g., SEP and SIMPLE)

questions.stem: A SIMPLE IRA sponsor has elected the 3 percent match. One employee earning $90,000 defers 10 percent and another earning $40,000 defers 2 percent. What does the employer contribute for the two of them?
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(p)(2)(A)(iii) makes the match dollar for dollar on what the employee actually defers, capped at the applicable percentage: 3 percent of $90,000 is $2,700 for the first employee, and the second's 2 percent deferral of $800 is matched in full because it is below the cap.
questions.pageTitle: Plans for self-employed persons (e.g., SEP and SIMPLE)

questions.stem: An employee covered by her employer's SEP wants to set aside more of her own pay for retirement than the employer contributes. What are her options within the SEP?
options: She may make salary reduction contributions to the SEP up to the elective deferral limit
She may elect to have the employer contribute more from her pay
None, because a SEP takes only employer money and the employee has no election, so she must use a separate IRA of her own
She may make after-tax contributions to the SEP that the employer must match
questions.explanation: Under IRC § 408(k) a SEP is funded by the employer alone; there is no salary reduction in a SEP, and the employee's only involvement is owning the IRA that receives the money.
questions.pageTitle: Plans for self-employed persons (e.g., SEP and SIMPLE)

questions.stem: A profit-sharing plan buys a warehouse from its sponsoring employer at a price supported by two independent appraisals. The plan has ample cash and the property is a sound investment. Has a prohibited transaction occurred?
options: No, because the price is fair and the plan is not harmed
Yes, because a sale of property between a plan and a disqualified person is prohibited regardless of price
No, because the employer is not a disqualified person unless it is also a fiduciary
Yes, but only if the plan later sells at a loss
questions.explanation: IRC § 4975(c)(1)(A) prohibits any sale or exchange of property between a plan and a disqualified person, and the employer is a disqualified person under IRC § 4975(e)(2)(C); appraisals go to the amount involved, not to whether the transaction is prohibited.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old's self-directed IRA had a balance of $200,000 on 1 January 2026 and $230,000 in October 2026, when she used IRA-owned property for a personal holiday without paying rent. What is the tax consequence?
options: A 15 percent initial tax on the amount involved, with a correction period
$200,000 is treated as distributed on 1 January 2026, taxed as ordinary income with the IRC § 72(t) additional tax on top
$230,000 is treated as distributed in October 2026
Nothing, provided she pays fair rent for the stay before the year ends
questions.explanation: IRC § 408(e)(2) provides that the account ceases to be an IRA as of the first day of the taxable year and is treated as distributing all its assets then, so the 1 January balance is taxed, and because she is under 59½ the IRC § 72(t) additional tax applies; there is no excise tax and no correction.

questions.stem: A sole proprietor sponsors a profit-sharing plan. Her son-in-law, who is neither a fiduciary nor a service provider to the plan, sells land to the plan at fair market value. Is he a disqualified person?
options: No, because in-laws are outside the family definition
Yes, because the spouse of a lineal descendant is a member of the family
No, because the price was fair
Yes, but only if the sole proprietor's daughter is also an employee
questions.explanation: IRC § 4975(e)(6) defines family as a spouse, ancestors, lineal descendants and the spouses of lineal descendants, so a son-in-law is a disqualified person and the sale is prohibited under IRC § 4975(c)(1)(A), whereas a sibling would not be caught by the family rule.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the three tax advantages that qualification under IRC § 401(a) secures?
options: The employer deducts its contribution when made
The employee is not taxed until distribution
The trust's earnings accumulate free of tax
Amounts distributed to the employee are received free of tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 402(a): an amount actually distributed by an exempt employees' trust is taxable to the distributee in the year distributed under IRC § 72. The three advantages are the IRC § 404 deduction on contribution, the IRC § 402(a) deferral until distribution, and tax-free accumulation under IRC § 501(a).

questions.stem: An executive's bonus is based on performance over calendar year 2026. On 20 August 2026, with no election in place, she elects to defer it under the company's non-qualified plan. She has participated in the plan for years. Is the election timely?
options: Yes, because it was made before the end of the performance period
Yes, because performance-based compensation may be deferred at any time before payment
No, because the election had to be made at least six months before the end of the twelve-month performance period
No, because performance-based compensation can never be deferred
questions.explanation: IRC § 409A(a)(4)(B): for performance-based compensation based on services over at least twelve months the election may be made no later than six months before the end of the period, which for calendar 2026 means by 30 June; the general prior-year rule and the thirty-day first-eligibility rule do not help her.

questions.stem: A participant takes an early distribution of $30,000 from his employer's qualified 401(k) plan with no exception available. Which additional tax applies?
options: 20 percent under IRC § 409A
10 percent under IRC § 72(t)
Both, because the two statutes are cumulative
None, because qualified plan distributions carry no additional tax
questions.explanation: IRC § 72(t): the 10 percent additional tax is the provision for an early distribution from a qualified plan. IRC § 409A polices non-qualified deferred compensation and does not apply to a qualified plan, so applying its 20 percent additional tax here has the wrong statute.
